### M. FABII QVINTILIANI ORATORIARVM INSTITVTIONVM LIBER VNDECIMVS.

->*De apte dicendo.*<-

NARRATA, sicut superiore libro continetur, facultate scribendi, cogitandiq;, & ex tempore etiam, cum res poscet, orandi, proxima est cura, ut dicamus apte, quam uirtutem elocutionis quartam Cicero demonstrat, quæq; est, meo quidem iudicio, maxime necessaria. Nam cum sit ornatus orationis uarius, & multiplex, conueniatq; alius alij, nisi fuerit accommodatus rebus, atque personis, non modo non illustrabit eam, sed & destruet, & uim rerum in contrarium uertet. Quid enim prodest esse uerba & latina, & significantia, & nitida, figuris etiam, numerisq; elaborata, nisi cum iis, in quæ iudicem duci, formariq; uolumus, consentiant? si genus sublime dicendi paruis in causis, paruum, limatumq; grandibus, lætum tristibus, lene asperis, minax supplicibus, summissum concitatis, trux, atque uiolentum iucundis adhibeamus, ut monilibus, & margaritis, ac ueste longa, quæ sunt ornamenta fœminarum, deformentur uiri, nec habitus triumphalis, quo nihil excogitari potest augustius, fœminas deceat. Hunc locum Cicero breuiter in tertio de oratore libro perstringit, neque tamen uideri potest quicquam omisisse, dicendo non omni causæ, nec auditori, nec personæ, nec tempori congruere orationis unum genus, nec fere pluribus in oratore eadem. sed illic L. Crassus, cum apud summos oratores, hominesq; eruditissimos dicat, satis habet partem hanc, uelut notare inter agnoscentes. Et hic Cicero alloquens Brutum testatur esse hæc ei nota. For this also happens: that thought calls us back to those worked-out passages and does not allow us to test the fortune of the moment; thus, the mind, wavering between the two, grows agitated, since it both loses what was written and does not seek new things. But a place has been destined for memory in the next book, and it should not be attached to this part, because there are other things that must be said by us first.

### THE ELEVENTH BOOK OF THE INSTITUTES OF ORATORY BY M. FABIUS QUINTILIANUS

-> *On Speaking Appropriately* <-

Having narrated, as is contained in the previous book, the faculty of writing, thinking, and even speaking extemporaneously when the situation demands it, the next concern is that we speak appropriately. Cicero demonstrates this as the fourth virtue of elocution, and it is, in my judgment, the most necessary. For although the embellishment of speech is varied and manifold, and one thing is suitable for one purpose and another for another, unless it is accommodated to the subject matter and the persons involved, it will not only fail to illuminate the speech but will destroy it and turn the force of the facts into the opposite. For what does it profit to have words that are Latin, significant, and polished, and even worked out with figures and rhythms, if they do not agree with those things to which we wish to lead and shape the judge? If we apply a sublime style of speaking to small cases, or a small and refined style to great ones; if we apply a cheerful style to sad matters, a gentle one to harsh ones, a threatening one to suppliants, a subdued one to excited ones, or a fierce and violent one to pleasant ones—it is as if men were to be deformed by necklaces and pearls and the long garments which are the ornaments of women, and as if the triumphal habit, than which nothing more august can be devised, were to suit women. Cicero briefly brushes upon this topic in the third book of *De Oratore*, nor can he be seen to have omitted anything, by saying that one type of speech does not suit every case, nor every listener, nor every person, nor every time, and that the same type rarely suits more than one in an orator. But there, L. Crassus, since he is speaking among the highest orators and most learned men, is satisfied to merely mark this part as if among those who already know it. And here, Cicero, addressing Brutus, testifies that these things are known to him. And therefore, it is handled more briefly by him...

Concerning which I wished to warn before the event, so that those things which happen naturally do not strike fear into anyone.

# Astrological Judgment concerning the Solar Eclipse.

Although I willingly refrain from astrological judgment, which, because of the concurrence of other causes that cancel out the effect of the stars, as a rule does not attain the event, especially at this time when men pressed on all sides by evils should rather be raised up than further terrified; yet because human curiosity, which is too intent on divinations, is only finally satisfied in the description of Eclipses when it thinks anxiously—even if they show some evil—about how to decline and escape it, and when the significations and events that accompany the Eclipse are added; I will subjoin a brief exposition of the more notable accidents which, according to the opinions of astrologers, will follow these labors of the Sun. This is especially so since this is a horrendous Eclipse, such as we have not had for many years, and it is a lunation that most closely precedes the entry of the Sun into Aries, to which Ptolemy, in a general judgment of the events of the year, commands us to look most of all.

All the ends of the earth have seen * the salvation of our God.

Vid quo quisque illorum tulerit: et si fortes fuerint tu talis fieri desidera: si muliebri et ignaue nihil perit aut digni sunt: quando desiderio ut tibi placeat: aut indigni quando desideret ignauia. Quid enim est turpius: quasi si maximi viri tudos fortiter moriendo faciunt? Laude toties dignu laudibusque dicas? Tanto fortior tanto felicior hominis effugisti casus: liuore moribus: eristi ex custodia: non tu dignus mala fortuna diis visus es: indignus que iam aliquod fortuna posset. Sub ducentibus vero se: et ipsa morte ad vitam respectantibus manus inijciende sunt. Nemine flebo letum: nemine flente. Ille lachrimas suas ipse abstersit: hic suis lachrimis effecit ne ullis dignus sit. Ego hercule fleam quem vivum viderim: aut Regulum quem tot clanis configit et transfigit: aut Catonem quem vulnera sua fortiter tulit? Omnis isti leui temporis impensa iuenerunt quo etni fieret: ad immortalitate moriendo venerunt. Est et illa solicitudini non mediocre materia: si te arte proponas: nec ullis simpliciter ostendas: qualis multum vita est ficta ostentatio pata. Torquet enim assidua obseruatio sui: et reprehendi alii quis solum metuit. nec unquam cura soluimur ut totiens nos existimari putem quotiens aspici. Nam et multa incidunt que inuitos denudent: et ut bene cedat tanta sui diligencia non tamen iucunda vita: aut secura est semper sub persona vicium. translation: and Cicero to offer his neck to his clients. That foolish Cato, leaning on his sword, at the same time to satisfy himself and the republic openly. Behold, also to pay the unjust rewards of fortune, and what each one now expects for himself when he sees the worst outcomes occurring. What, therefore, is it? See what each of them bore, and if they were strong, desire to become such; if womanish and cowardly, nothing is lost, either they are worthy when you desire that it may please you, or they are unworthy when cowardice desires it. For what is more shameful than if the greatest men do their duty by dying bravely? Should you speak of them with praises as often as they are worthy of praise? So much stronger, so much happier, you have escaped the accidents of man, envy, and customs, you have emerged from the prison; you have not seemed to the gods worthy of bad fortune, you have been unworthy of whatever fortune could now do. But against those leading themselves, and looking back at life even in death, hands must be laid. I will weep for no one who is happy, for no one who is weeping. The former wiped away his own tears; the latter, by his own tears, ensured that he is worthy of nothing. Should I, by Hercules, weep for him whom I have seen alive, or for Regulus, whom so many disasters configure and transconfigure, or for Cato, who bore his own wounds bravely? All of these gained a small expenditure of time to become eternal; they reached immortality by dying. And there is also that not mediocre material for anxiety, if you propose yourself in art, and do not show yourself simply, such as the life of many is a feigned ostentation. For the continuous observation of oneself tortures, and one fears that he will be criticized by another. Nor are we ever freed from care, as we think we are being judged as often as we are seen. For many things happen that uncover us against our will, and even if it turns out well, such diligence of self is not, however, a pleasant life, or secure; it is always behind the mask of vice. Fourth, [a person] omits theft by despoiling the republic, and this is called <term>peculatus</term> <gloss>embezzlement of public funds</gloss>, as in the 22nd Question, 3rd Chapter, "Quod g.," where it is added: "Embezzlement, indeed, is theft from the republic." It follows that it is not indicated as theft of private property, but of the public. Therefore, it is asked what is to be said regarding those who turn public monies or other public things into their own. To this it must be said that, beyond [the fact that] things should be punished by capital penalty according to the laws, as in the Institutes, "De publicis iudiciis," the Julian Law of Embezzlement, because he who mixes iron or similar [materials] with public gold or silver [is guilty]. As in the final law, "Ad legem Iuliam peculatus." Similarly, a public moneyer who stamps public currency and retains [some] for himself, as in the law "Sacrilegis," chapter of the same. Public officials who hold the seal and do not account for the florins, and these [men] damaging the republic, fall into embezzlement, as in the argument regarding the law "Ad legem Iuliam peculatus." Similarly, he who damages the republic by damaging or changing a book or writing concerning the measurement of fields or a public road, as in the law "Quod tabulas," in the Digest, "Ad legem Iuliam peculatus." Similarly, he who damages the republic by feigning creditors of the treasury and receiving money from the treasury which should be private property, as in the Digest, "Ad legem Iuliam peculatus," law "Sacrilegis," of the same chapter. Similarly, public officials selling [offices] and dictators are held to restitution of money, even if not to those who gave [it], if they are poor, and those purchasing illicitly wish to be punished by the gravity of the Julian Law on Bribery, law "Unica," in the Digest, "Ad legem Iuliam ambitus," Institutes "De publicis iudiciis." [These are the things] furthermore, and these, for their sons, judgment must be had. But those who justly serve the republic, if they were to serve for a time for their own private gain with the monies of the republic, they would not sin, provided that the republic was in no way burdened or suffered damage, for instance, in that it would be burdened for all that time; otherwise, it would remain intact and not applied to anyone or for any utility. For all who bring damage to the republic, for example, by falsifying currency in weight, form, or common standard, or by diminishing [the quality] for gain, or [falsifying] gold or silver, and these [people] and others who are simply purifying [the metal], and those who with various measures, weights, and measures falsify, are called thieves of the republic, as in the Digest, "De contrahenda emptione," law 1; and such thieves are punished by the laws in boiling water, as in the Digest, "De falsa moneta," law 2, and such currency does not deserve to be paid, Digest "De pignoribus," law "Eleganter." In this lot also are counted merchants who agree among themselves that goods are given at a certain price, specifically that many are sold for a higher price, or that only one person may sell certain goods, for those who exercise such an office and those laws should all be despoiled of their goods and punished with perpetual exile. Similarly, those approaching and admitting it should be punished, as in the Code "De monopoliis," law "Una," and it is no wonder, because such [people] most greatly damage the city and are held to the restitution of all that they received for more than a just price. Of which detestable theft it is to move the boundaries of a neighbor, of which it is written, Deuteronomy 21: "Cursed is he who moves the boundaries of his neighbor," which is principally understood as the great extension of someone’s field and the unjust usurpation of anyone’s property. To the praise of God.

Regarding the restitution of theft in the last four modes, namely in sacrilege, in [items] found in the use of another's thing, and in hidden retention [or] unjust [retention of] justly acquired [things]. Sermon 9. <note>Large red decorative initial O</note>On theft, Exodus 20. Having discussed the four first differing [types] of theft, now let us pursue the rest. The fifth, indeed, is the theft they commit by which they incur sacrilege, which itself aggravates the theft not insignificantly, as Augustine says on John, and it is held in the 22nd Question, 3rd Chapter, "Quod g.," which is not indicated as theft of private property, but of the republic, as appears in the following law. "How much more vehemently is the sacrilegious thief to be judged, not just anyone, but [he who] steals from the church, [for] anyone who steals something from the church is entirely to be condemned, because he was a thief of sacred vessels and holy places," as it is promised in the same place. For which it must be known that sacrilege is whenever someone violates the sacred, either by taking the sacred from the sacred, or the profane from the profane, or the profane from the sacred, or the sacred from the profane, as is held in the 15th Question, 3rd Chapter, "Hi quis contumax," question "Sacrilegium," where it is added that sacrilege sustains double penalty, namely pecuniary and of excommunication, and according to the gloss, the first is for the damage suffered, the second is for the immunity of the church violated.

translation: up to here Pliny. And the palm, as the gloss touches upon over the Psalm <note>a reference to Psalm 92:12 "The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree"</note>, is a tree of great height; but yet it does not reach to the height of a cedar, whose root is rough and round, very fixed in the depth of the earth. Its trunk, however, is leafy and compact and of incorruptible strength. Its bark upon the trunk is hard and rugose and in some way stinging, and most especially towards the earth, and therefore it is difficult to climb, and with difficulty one arrives at its fruit. Its leaves have a pyramidal form in the manner of a sword. Although, however, the palm is hard around the stem and rough in the upper parts, yet it is of joyful aspect in the beauty of its branches, and in the crown at the summit of the branches it carries its fruits and not in the middle of the leaves, as Pliny says, book 13, whose fruit is so much the more unctuous, sweeter, and more digestive the more immediately it approaches the rays of the sun. It grows in many regions, but it does not fruit as it does in the region scorched by the spikes of the sun, in level, sandy, and vitreous soil; and therefore the palm of Judea is renowned, as Pliny says, book 13, chapter 5. Item, in the same place, the species of palms is twofold: male and female. The male flowers first, the female afterwards bursts forth into the germ; nor does the female fruit unless it is so near to the male that at least the wind mediates and the female is impregnated by the scent of the male. In the same place, the Philosopher says in his book of <term>Vegetables</term> <note>refers to Aristotle's De Plantis</note>, that when it is sown, it is necessary that the seeds of male and female be sown together, and the female should be composed two by two, and from the individuals the plant erupts, whence four plantlets coalesce from them, which cohere so much to each other and bind themselves mutually by a wondrous artifice of nature in the manner of a net. Nor does the female grow well, nor even fruit without the male; nay, if the male tree is cut down, the female after two years becomes sterile. But with the rough leaves and flowers of the male around the roots of the female, the female receives and resumes strength again as if from intercourse by the proximity of the male. Nor do such plantings like a place that is humid, fat, and smoky, but rather a place that is salty and sandy, and therefore where there is no such soil, it is necessary that salt be sprinkled, not near the root, but somewhat in the vicinity, so that by such saltiness the superfluity of the humors of the earth is consumed; and Pliny says there is a certain species of palm in the meridian, it is believed to be one, and no other is multiplied from it, but when by age it completely perishes and fails, it is born again from itself and revives, and therefore it is said that the phoenix, the bird of Arabia, received its name from the shrub of this plant or palm, because when it dies, it is said to revive, as Pliny says in the same place. Item, in the same place, the author says there are different species of palms in Ethiopia, marvelous not so much for greenness as for sweetness and for juice and speed; for their fruits are most rich in juice, whence also the best wine is expressed from them, up to here Pliny, book 18, chapter 5. The palm is therefore a singular tree, slender in the stem and hairy, in respect to the leaf from which it exits, but beautiful and dilated in the branches and foliage in respect to the heaven, to which it extends itself at its summit. Its leaves are long, in surface indeed small and thick and flexible, for various connections, being very suitable for baskets, as Jerome says; nevertheless, in the lateral angles they are incisive and sharp. Its branches are called <term>elate</term> <gloss>branches/raised things</gloss>, that is, raising themselves upward, keeping a continuous greenness, and never inclining themselves from the lowest. And according to this, the middle of this division of <term>elate</term> in the penultimate has it long, as Canticles 5 says: "Your hair is like the palm tree." <note>original: "Come tua elate palmarum"</note>. Elate, however, or <term>elates</term> in Greek is called <term>abies</term> <gloss>fir tree</gloss> in Latin, and according to this, the penultimate is shortened, and thus it seems to place another text which says in Canticles 5: "His hair as a fir tree" <note>original: "crines eius sicut abies"</note>, as the author says, and thus the middle has to be shortened, not lengthened; however, the fruit of the palm is varied as much in form as in virtue, according to the diversity of the wood from which it exits, and according to the diversity of the soil in which the palm grows, and according to the various reception of celestial heat which diffuses itself in diverse ways according to the diverse sites to the summits of the palms, as Pliny says, book 13. The first is clear, for in many palms, fruit is rarely or never found because of the bad or less than sufficient disposition of the tree itself, as is evident in Italian palms in which rarely or never is any fruit found; and if it grows, it is never found to reach maturity and due completion, as Pliny says. The second is clear from what was said before, why in soil or earth that is too cold and humid, fat or smoky and easy, they do not succeed, nay, they do not grow at all by any remedy, as the same author says. The third is also evident, that in shady places, removed from the presence of the rays of the sun, palms cannot grow; and if by chance they have grown elsewhere, they can in no way reach the glory of palms by fruiting. And this is what Plato <note>again, likely a general attribution to medical/philosophical authority</note> touches upon in the <term>Diet</term>. Dates, he says, that is, palm-bearing fruits, are cold and humid in the second degree, and have diverse actions according to the various qualities of the regions. For some are born in a cold region, that is, remotely cold; some in a hot one; some, however, in between these, temperate. Those, however, in a hot region, where there is continuous fruit, are very sweet in taste and by some viscosity somewhat unctuous, and yet, since they are very sweet, if anyone uses them too much, they cause obstructions and opilations of the stomach and also of the head, and of the pathways of the spleen and liver, from which it is evident that it is not good to use all sweet things continuously; nay, it is more often harmful to the soul and body. But fruits growing in cold or remotely cold land do not arrive at maturity, and therefore remaining in their pungency and dryness, they are green; although they somewhat strengthen the stomach, yet they are not easily received by the stomach. Whence, causing delay there, they generate twistings of the gut more often and introduce them, as the same author says. Growing

->### Argumentum ep. 15.<-

*Prima pars epistolae Pompeium vituperat, Caesarem laudat. orto enim ciuili bello, tutiorem partem, non honestiorem, Coelius elegerat: ut re ipsa comprobaret, quod scripserat epistola proxima, his verbis: Illud te non arbitror fugere, quin homines in dissensione domestica debeant, quam diu ciuiliter sine armis certetur, honestiorem sequi partem; ubi ad bellum, et castra ventum sit, firmiorem; et id melius statuere, quod tutius sit. Subiungit de sua cupiditate conveniendi, et alloquendi Ciceronis: de itinere ad Alpes: de Domitio, Caesaris hospite, interfecto. Scripsit autem hanc epistolam anno sequenti post superiores, id est, Lentulo, et Marcello cos. Meminit enim in extrema epistola de Domitio Ahenobarbo, Corfinij a Caesare capto, et dimisso.*

but he might place a limit on possessions, concerning which matters Appius was acting very vehemently in the senate, so that the consuls might bring it forward. <note>Cicero to Atticus, the last letter of book 6</note>. **Censorship is like fuller's earth or soda.**] Censorship is able to wipe away filth in such a way that fuller's earth <note>original: "lomentum" — a cosmetic scrub used to remove skin blemishes</note> removes wrinkles; or it can wash them away, just as stains are washed from garments with soda: that is, he thinks that by the diligence and severity of the censorship, the infamy of those vices can be removed with which one previously defiled oneself shamefully. <note>Philippics 1</note>: "However dirty each one shall appear, so most willingly will he wash away his filth by the severity of judging." That stains are accustomed to be removed by soda, that passage of the prophet Jeremiah indicates, chapter 2. "If you wash yourself with soda, and multiply for yourself the herb of the ox <note>original: "herbam bouis" — likely referring to soapwort</note>: you are spotted in your iniquity before me, says the Lord God." Touching upon which passage blessed Jerome, epistle 47, says: "One must beware of the stain which, according to Jeremiah, can be washed away by no soda, by no herb of the fullers." **He opens the bowels**] He is so far from erasing the old opinion of men regarding his vices that, with this severity, he stirs it up even more vehemently. **At the house of Drusus**] <term>Livius Drusus</term> the praetor, than whom no one committed more against the Scantinian Law. Perhaps he is the one who is named in letter 16, book 4, to Atticus: and who was the mother of Livia, who later married Augustus. **Appius**] ill-spoken of for the sake of those things concerning which he acts most vehemently. **Curio**] tribune of the plebs. **He relaxed regarding the pay of Pompeius**] At this time Curio was the fiercest adversary to the optimates and Pompeius. He was therefore interceding so that a decree of the senate might not be made concerning paying the salary to the legions of Pompeius. <note>Epistle 4</note>. **Parthian war**] For with Crassus having been killed along with the Roman legions, the Parthians were threatening the neighboring Roman provinces: against whom it seemed that either Caesar or Pompeius, who stood out in the glory of military affairs, should be sent. <note>Epistle 8, and the last letter of book 7 to Atticus</note>. **He will judge.**] As if by the judgment and opinion of arms their discord will be settled. My book has "He will vindicate" <note>original: "Vindicabit"</note>; one of Sigonius has "He has vindicated" <note>original: "Vindicauit"</note>. **Without the highest danger**] The sentiment is neither obscure nor absurd. However, I think it must be considered diligently why in all the clearly ancient books, for "highest" <note>original: "Summo"</note>, it is written "his own" <note>original: "Suo"</note>. From which I suspect that a conjecture has arisen that "your" <note>original: "Tuo"</note> should be read, which is in certain Transalpine books. **Pleasant**] There can be no struggle between citizens pleasant to a good man, even if it be without danger. But Caelius speaks according to his own nature.

->### Argument of Letter 15.<-

*The first part of the letter criticizes Pompeius and praises Caesar. For, with the civil war having arisen, Caelius had chosen the safer side, not the more honorable one: so that he might prove in fact what he had written in the previous letter, in these words: "I do not think it escapes you that men in domestic dissension ought, as long as it is contested civilly without arms, to follow the more honorable side; when it has come to war and camps, the stronger one; and to decide that better which is safer." He adds regarding his desire to meet and speak with Cicero: regarding his journey to the Alps: and regarding Domitius, Caesar's guest, being killed. He wrote this letter in the year following the previous ones, that is, in the consulship of Lentulus and Marcellus. For he mentions at the end of the letter Domitius Ahenobarbus, captured at Corfinium by Caesar and released.*

->### M. Caelius sends greetings to M. Cicero. 15.<-

Have you ever seen a man more inept than your Gnaeus Pompeius, who stirred up such turmoils, who was so trivial? Or have you read or heard of anyone more keen in carrying out affairs than our Caesar, yet more temperate in victory? What is it? Now do our soldiers, who finished the war by marching through the hardest and coldest places in the most foul winter, seem to you to have been fed on round cakes? What? "Already," you say, "everything is glorious." If you knew how anxious I am, then you would deride this glory of mine, which concerns me not at all. Which I cannot explain to you except in person: and I hope that will be soon. For when he had driven Pompeius from Italy, he decided to summon me to the city: which I think is already accomplished: unless he preferred to besiege Pompeius at Brundisium.

<column-break/>

May I die if there is the slightest reason for me to hurry there, other than that I desire to see you and discuss all inner matters. I have, however, so many things. Alas, I fear, as is accustomed to happen, that when I have seen you, I shall forget everything. But yet, what kind of wickedness has made it necessary for me to take a journey back toward the Alps? It is because the Intemelii <note>a Ligurian tribe</note> are in arms, and not for a great cause. Bellienus, a home-born slave of Demetrius, who was there with a garrison, seized and strangled a certain Domitius, a nobleman there and a guest of Caesar, after money was accepted from the opposing faction. The state is going to arms. I must go there now with cohorts through the snows. "Everywhere," you say, "the Domitii are giving themselves trouble." I would indeed wish that he who was born of Venus had had as much spirit in your Domitius as he himself had in this one. Greetings to Cicero's son. Farewell.

Thus, they taught all Sciences, both Mundane <note>of this world</note> and Supramundane <note>beyond the physical world, such as spiritual or celestial realms</note>, through the properties of essential numbers. Later, they were mocked by others because they believed that physical substances could be produced from numbers and bare quantities. These critics did not sufficiently understand the intent of such great Philosophers, nor did they grasp the properties and powers of essential numbers. 

Truly, if the numbers of parts are constant and perpetual, and if the proportions and orderly **Mixtures** <term>Mixture (Mixtio): Not a random blending, but a specific, balanced combination of elemental qualities that creates a stable organ or substance.</term> of numbers in the liturgy <note>original: "lithurgia"; here meaning the 'work' or 'orderly service' of nature's processes</note> of Generations do not happen by chance, nor after the fact, they must instead be contained within that **Mechanical Science** <term>Mechanical Science (Scientia Mechanica): Here, the author refers to the divine or natural "engineering" of the universe—the precise, structural laws by which God or Nature builds physical forms.</term> about which we have already spoken so often, where magnitudes, shapes, colors, flavors, and other **signatures** <term>Signatures (signaturę): The belief that the physical appearance of a thing (its color, shape, or smell) reveals its inner properties and medicinal uses.</term> are established. 

But if these numbers are contained within this Science, they will not be idle, but vital and full of power; they will explain the orderly proportions in these progressions and provide proof that all things have been created by weight, measure, and order <note>A reference to the Wisdom of Solomon 11:20: "thou hast ordered all things in measure and number and weight."</note>. <meta>This page continues Cardinal Bessarion’s critique of George of Trebizond’s translation of Plato’s Laws. Bessarion is currently identifying specific philological errors and misunderstandings of Greek idioms regarding civic hospitality and historical events.</meta>

### BOOK [V]

<margin>Education</margin>
...that the Cretan says his ancestors left Athens. This man [the Interpreter] relates that Epimenides and other Cretans were once guests in Athens. Here, because the Athenians, upon the approach of the Persian army, deserted their city and took to their ships, he says the Cretans "left the city." He thinks that the Greek word <term>xenousthai</term> <note>original: "ξενοῦσθαι"</note> means "to be alienated" when in this context it clearly signifies "to be hosted" or "to be bound by the custom of hospitality."

Likewise, Plato judges that education must first be defined, and its power must be sought. To this sentiment he adds: "for we think that we must proceed by way of it [education] in this discussion which we have established." The Interpreter says: "for it is necessary to go through her, of whom we have just spoken." <note>The Interpreter uses "her" as if referring back to a person rather than the concept of education.</note>

Likewise, Plato perceived that everyone ought to practice from childhood that in which they strive to excel others. Im-

<margin>What must be applied to tender minds</margin>
mediately, he says, "one must practice this same thing, whether one must study agriculture, or carpentry, or any other art, and the tools and instruments—small replicas of the true and complete forms—must be applied in those still-tender years by the one who has undertaken the care of instruction." The Interpreter says: "or to fashion certain instruments of agriculture which, though useless, nevertheless contribute not a little to the imitation of useful and true instruments." While this might not seem inelegantly put in Latin, it nevertheless recedes far from the author's meaning.

Again, Plato says regarding the education of the young: **"I say the main point of education is right upbringing, which leads the soul of the one playing, as much as possible, into a love for that which he will need to be perfect in the virtue of the matter when he has become a man."** <note>original: "κεφάλαιον δὴ παιδείας λέγω μὲν φησὶ, τὴν ὀρθὴν τροφὴν, ἣ τῷ παίζοντος τὴν ψυχὴν, εἰς ἔρωτα ὅ τι μάλιστα ἄξει τούτου, ὃ δεήσει γενόμενον, αὐτὸν τὸν τέλειον εἶναι τῆς τῶ πράγματος ἀρετῆς."</note>

<margin>Right Education / Education snatched away</margin>
"The 'head' of education," he says, "we establish as the right method of upbringing, which—while the boy is still playing—draws his mind toward the love of that thing which, having reached manhood, can make him perfect by its virtue." The Interpreter says: "the 'head' of the teaching of infants is nourishment, which will lead the mind of those playing to seek that which we have decreed they should use in manhood." What kind of "nourishment" this might be, which has such great power that it makes a man excel in virtue, I do not see—especially since "the nourishment of infants," as the Interpreter calls it, is milk. Indeed, there is no need to ask what he has added or taken away in this passage. The Interpreter seems to think he is rightly correcting Plato when, by changing everything, he sets things out "more wisely and ornately"; and because <term>trophe</term> <note>Bessarion notes a confusion here; the Greek word *trophe* can mean both 'upbringing/education' and 'nourishment/food'.</note> among the Greeks signifies both the education of the mind and the nourishment of the body, he preferred to say "nourishment" rather than "education," being ignorant that the second meaning fits this passage so well that the first is utterly absurd.

Furthermore, Plato, when discussing the passions and the reason of the soul, says: **"One must assist the most beautiful guidance of the law; since reason, being noble but mild and not violent, requires helpers for its guidance."** <note>original: "Δεῖ δὴ τῆ καλλίστη ἀγωγῆ τῆ τῶ νόμου ξυλλαμβάνειν· ἅτε τὸ τῶ λογισμοῦ καλοῦ μὲν ὄντος, πρᾶος δὲ καὶ οὐ βιαίου, δεῖσθαι ὑπηρετῶν αὐτῷ τῶ ἀγωγὴν."</note> "Therefore," he says, "reason must be helped by the most beautiful institution of the law, so that it may indeed be able to conquer the passions. For since reason itself is good, but gentle and not at all violent, it requires the service of an assistant."

<margin>Conquering the passions</margin>
The Interpreter says: "it is necessary, therefore, to follow the best guidance of the law. For since reasoning is good, and also mild and not violent, it has need of guidance for itself, like a servant."

Likewise, Plato says: **"We can understand two forms of fear, which are almost opposites."** <note>original: "Δύο φόβων εἴδη, σχεδὸν ἐναντία δυνάμεθα κατανοῆσαι."</note> "Two kinds of fearing," he says, "almost contrary to each other, we can observe." The Interpreter omitted the word "contrary," in which word the whole force of the meaning lies. For we fear either because of horrific things or because of shameful things,

<margin>We fear</margin>
and he asks whether two kinds of fear can be understood. Likewise, Plato inquires in what way someone can be made "timid" and be held back by the fear of all things which are rightly to be feared, and so he asks: **"What else do we attempt in order to make someone fearful with justice?"** <note>original: "Τί δ' ἔτ' ἐπιχειρεῖ μεν τινα φοβερὸν ποιεῖν μετὰ δίκης."</note> "How most aptly do we attempt to make someone timid?"

<margin>The Timid</margin>
The Interpreter says: "What furthermore, when we desire to make someone rightly to be feared?"—which meaning is plainly contrary to the meaning of Plato.

Again, Plato, explaining the way in which someone can most aptly be made timid: **"Is it not by bringing him into contact with things that are not dangerous, and training him beforehand, that we must make him conquer by fighting against his pleasures?"** <note>original: "Ἆρ' οὐκ ἀκινδύνω ξυμβάλλοντας αὐτὸν, καὶ προγυμνάζοντας, νικᾶν δεῖ ποιεῖν, διαμαχόμενον αὐτῷ τοῖς ἡδοναῖς."</note> "Is it not," he says, "by moving him toward things that are less than modest, that we shall resolve to test and exercise him, and so accustom him to overcome pleasures by fighting?" The Interpreter says: "Do we not, by casting him into impudence, urge him to conquer either his pleasures or his fortitude in a fight?"

<margin>Impudence</margin>
Indeed, I am certain that a man whom the Interpreter has cast "into impudence" (to use his words) ought not to conquer his own fortitude in a fight; for fortitude of mind must be preserved by one who wishes to conquer pleasure or an enemy. Why the adversary would have said the opposite, or what he finally wants for himself, I do not sufficiently understand.

Then Plato says: "I was speaking of two fears, one of which is contrary to pains, and also contrary to many and the greatest pleasures." He is speaking of both of these regarding that time which arises from shame, saying these words: **"I was speaking of two fears; of which one is contrary to pains and other fears, and is contrary to most and the greatest pleasures."** <note>original: "δυό ἔλεγον φόβους· ὧν ὁ ἕτερος, ἐναντίος μὲν τοῖς ἀλγηδόσιν, ἢ τοῖς ἄλλοις φόβοις· ἐναντίος δ' ἐστὶ τοῖς πλείστοις, καὶ μεγίσταις ἡδοναῖς."</note>

His companion responds: **"Not so far as can happen by probable reason."** <note>original: "οὐκοῦν τὸν γ' εἰκότα λόγον ἂν ἔχοι."</note> The Interpreter joins this response of the companion with Plato's question, and by adding certain things...

## *On investigating the distribution of vessels, ureters, and nerves in the kidneys.*
### Chapter XLIII.

Once these procedures have been correctly and properly performed, it will be the right time to follow the kidney's own <term>tunica: a natural covering or coat of an organ</term> with your scalpel. This membrane should already be pulled back and stripped away. Use one hand to grasp the <term>emulgent: an old term for the renal vessels</term> vessels, the urinary vessel <note>the ureter</note>, and the nerves that you previously tied. Follow where the scalpel leads you. This membrane is a single and continuous structure. It passes through along with these vessels and expands within the fissure. This occurs in the concave region of the kidneys where the substance appears divided and loosened on both sides. This area is quite large and penetrates deeply. As soon as the membrane is pulled back, it reveals an abundance of fat. The amount of fat present is always determined by the overall condition of the person's body. If you wipe and scrape this fat away, the kidney substance will appear uneven and as if it has been eroded. This is not because this part is naturally different from the rest. Rather, it is because of the divisions of the large vessels located there. It cannot appear as continuous and uniform as the substance found in the convex part of the kidneys. That convex area is filled everywhere with extremely thin branches of vessels that almost escape the sight. For this reason, I suspect most anatomists have asserted that the substance of the kidneys is sponge-like and cavernous. After this, consider carefully how that same membrane of the kidney is reflected and expanded. Notice how elegantly and fittingly it receives the branches of the vessels. Indeed, the branches themselves spread out above and below like the toes of a goose, supported by that same membrane.

# GERMANIÆ PROSPERITAS.

One could make a trial of the same thing with worms originating from meat or cheese, and one will discover that this saltpeter is not denied to animals here. Therefore, nothing will be found in which that universal Salt of the World is not discovered. In some, however, the salt more quickly assumes the nature of saltpeter, while in others it has already been made saltpeter by Nature.

Let this be an example: the Essential or universal salt of vegetables, animals, and minerals is indeed naturally nitrous, but it does not catch flame until it has attracted life and flame from the air. However, one of the salts attracts that life more quickly and readily than another, just as it was formed by Nature. The more fleeting and urinous the salts are, the more quickly they change themselves into niter. The more biting and corrosive they are, the more difficultly and slowly they assume the nature of saltpeter. But because niter is a salt participating in both natures, namely urinous and corrosive, and is as it were composed of both, that is, of urinous and corrosive salt, the skilled man will easily assist nature with its aid and will make of them whatever he wills. Nor is there any salt in the nature of things that cannot be changed into niter with the help of art; especially those salts that are sublimated by fire and, raised by its force, ascend: such as those that are in the urine and excrements of all animals: indeed, animals, vegetables, and minerals themselves quite easily seize the nature of Niter. Let this be the first grade of salts. The second grade is of those salts that are somewhat more fixed, as the sons of art...

# ON THE DUTIES OF PREFECTS BOOK III. PART I.

<margin>Chapter 2, verses 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10.</margin>
...we speak regarding the intention and genuine purpose of Paul's words; likewise, the same is clear from what the *Corinthians*, in accordance with this Pauline admonition, did toward this brother of *theirs*, who had caused that *scandal* to the Church. They had rebuked him in public, they had severed the bond of charity and of their own communion previously maintained with him, they held his sin against him <note>original: *peccatum ipsi reservaverunt*, meaning they did not grant him absolution</note>, and thus they had left him in a state of *extreme grief and sorrow*: all of which can be concluded from the *Second Epistle to the Corinthians*. But what do these things mean, other than that this man had truly been Excommunicated—that is, separated from Ecclesiastical communion by a public sentence of Paul and the Church, until he had shown clear signs of repentance? 

However, Erastus <note>Thomas Erastus (1524–1583) was a Swiss physician and theologian who argued that the Church did not have the scriptural authority to exclude people from the sacraments.</note> objects that not even a word is read here (nor elsewhere) regarding this man being barred or excluded by the sentence of the Church from the use of the Sacred Symbols of communion, *the bread and the wine*. Erastus constantly harps on this same string <note>original: *hac chorda... oberrat*, a musical metaphor for repeating a flawed argument</note>, and fights along these lines—to use the words of Tertullian <note>An influential early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155–220 AD).</note>—and he repeats this same objection to other passages as well, whether cited so far or to be cited below, which might seem to deal with *Excommunication*; therefore, it would be wrong to overlook this evasion. 

I grant Erastus, then, that this specific part or type of *Excommunication*, by which someone is barred from the use of the Sacred Symbols of the *bread and wine*, is not directly addressed in the writings of the New Testament; and I also confess that I have perceived this more clearly from the Erastians. Yet, even with this conceded, *Excommunication* as it is now received is not undermined. For the *exclusion* from the use of the *Sacred Symbols* must be considered a necessary and indubitable consequence of *Excommunication* as it was practiced in the age of the Apostles. 

For *Apostolic Excommunication* consisted in the same thing as *Jewish excommunication*: that someone should be separated from the communion of their brothers, and consequently also be excluded from the *Place* where that communion was practiced, and from the *Sacred Rites* <note>original: *Sacris*</note> celebrated there. Thus, *Excommunication* truly and properly consisted only in this: that someone was separated from the sacred assembly, as was the custom in the *Synagogue*. From this, however, it necessarily followed that the person was at the same time barred from the Symbols of Sacred communion. For it would be absurd to offer the Symbols of Sacred communion to one who, by the sentence of the Elders <note>original: *Presbyterorum*</note>, had been declared unworthy of the very communion of the brothers. It would have been absurd to sit with him at the *sacred table*, when it was not permitted to sit at a *common* [private] table...

-> OF PLANTS <-

Some, like duckweed, only float upon the waters, without any root at all; such as malabathrum, the leaf of Indian Nard, which Dioscorides mentions in his first book.

Some have knotty roots, such as the kinds of Satyrium, Aristolochia, and all kinds of Bulbs.

Some have tender roots, such as Ozymon.

<header>BOOK THREE.</header>

...Albinus and Quintus Martius Philippus were consuls, in the year 568 from the founding of the city, as Livy relates in the ninth book of the fourth decade. But to the magnificence of these works, let the luxury of the baths now be added. It was the custom of the ancients to bathe daily, a practice which, I believe, according to Celsus, contributes to maintaining good health. From this usage, it came about that every citizen, according to his wealth, had private baths. But later, with the growing luxury of the princes, public baths began to be held; indeed, places were assigned that offered the use of bathing or sweating, either by hot waters or by fire, which they called in Greek <term>thermae</term> <gloss>baths</gloss>. Both elsewhere and at Rome, they seemed to be constructed in the manner of provinces, as Ammianus says, in which even the common people might bathe. It was so popular for princes to bathe indiscriminately with the public that Capitolinus reports that Commodus, Gordian, and the younger Galen bathed three, five, or even seven times a day in summer, and twice in winter, and dined in the baths. Women were also admitted, a convenient instrument for pleasure. The baths most celebrated at Rome were the Agrippine, Neronian, Titi Vespasiani, Domitian, Antonine, Alexandrian, Gordian, Severian, Diocletian, Aurelian, Constantinian, and Novatian. These were built at great expense, almost like cities. In them were very ample courtyards, porticos, and in the porticos were <term>exedrae</term> <gloss>recessed alcoves</gloss> containing seats, in which philosophers, rhetoricians, and others who cared for studies sat debating. There was also a <term>palaestra</term> <gloss>wrestling school/gymnasium</gloss> in which athletes exercised. Moreover, there were many places inside skillfully constructed for fostering luxury. To such insane madness do the Roman princes seem to have sought the temptations of all pleasures, with such great expenditure benefiting so few.

The other lens at D is concave or convex, for either form of the telescope is suitable for this purpose, and indeed that which is of two convexes is more so, since it exhibits erect pictures, whereas the other inverts them. The point K of lens D becomes the meeting point or the dispersal point of the parallel rays coming from the side where H is, and a white board is set at H to receive the Sun's image. Therefore, so that it may appear distinct and well-defined, it is necessary that the rays which proceed from one point of the Sun, that is, which are carried parallel to each other into lens AB, be gathered again at one point on the board. ### O R A T I O.

I now omit Numerius, Serranus, and Aelius, the dregs of the Clodian sedition. Yet these, too, even now flutter about, as you see; and as long as you fear anything regarding yourselves, they will never fear for themselves. For why should I speak of the aedile himself? That man, who attacked, razed, and burned public monuments, sacred temples, and the homes of his enemies; who was always surrounded by assassins, hemmed in by armed men, and protected by informers, of whom there is a redundancy today; who incited a foreign band of criminals, and bought slaves fit for slaughter, and emptied the entire prison into the forum during his tribunate—he flutters about as aedile, he accuses the man who in some measure repressed his exultant fury. This man, who protected himself in such a way that he defended his household gods in private matters, and the rights and auspices of the tribunate in the republic; he was not allowed by the authority of the senate to be accused moderately by the man by whom he himself is nefariously accused. # The Tragicall History of

Where is it now? It is gone.
And see where God stretches forth his arm
And bends his ireful brows!
Mountains and hills, come, come, and fall on me,
And hide me from the heavy wrath of God!
No, no! Then will I headlong run into the earth.
Earth, gape! O, no, it will not harbor me.
You stars that reigned at my nativity,
Whose influence has allotted death and hell,
Now draw up Faustus like a foggy mist
Into the entrails of yon laboring cloud,
That when you vomit forth into the air,
My limbs may issue from your smoky mouths,
So that my soul may but ascend to heaven!
Ah, half the hour is past! The watch strikes.
It will all be past anon.
O God, if thou wilt not have mercy on my soul,
Yet, for Christ's sake, whose blood has ransomed me,
Impose some end to my incessant pain!
Let Faustus live in hell a thousand years,
A hundred thousand, and at last be saved.
O, no end is limited to damned souls!
Why wert thou not a creature wanting soul?
O, why is this immortal that thou hast?
Ah, Pythagoras's metempsychosis—were that true,
<note>Metempsychosis: The doctrine of the transmigration of souls.</note>
This soul should fly from me, and I be changed
Into some brutish beast. All beasts are happy, for when they die,
Their souls are soon dissolved in elements,
But mine must live still to be plagued in hell!
Cursed be the parents that engendered me!
No, Faustus, curse thyself, curse Lucifer
That has deprived thee of the joys of heaven.
The clock strikes twelve.
O, it strikes, it strikes! Now, body, turn to air,
Or Lucifer will bear thee quick to hell!
Thunder and lightning.

->LION AND LITTLE JACKAL<-

At another time there was a meeting of the animals, and Lion was the chief at the meeting. Little Jackal wanted to attend, but there was a law made that no one should be present unless he had horns. So Little Jackal took wax out of a nest of bees, and made horns for himself with it. He fastened the horns on his head, and went to the meeting. Lion did not know him on account of the horns. But he sat near the fire and went to sleep, when the horns melted.

Lion looked at him and saw who it was. He immediately tried to catch him, but Little Jackal was quick in springing away. He ran under an overhanging rock and sang out: "Help! help! this rock is falling upon me!"

Lion went for a pole to prop up the rock that he might get at Little Jackal. While he was away, Little Jackal escaped.

After that they became companions again, and went hunting another time. They killed an ox. Lion said: "I will watch it while you carry the pieces away."

Lion gave him the breast, and said: "Take this to my wife."

Philosophy, despairing of translating life by the rational method, in terms of inertia, is attempting to apprehend the universal flux by the aid of intuition. In brief, there is a renascence of *wonder*; and art must attune itself to this new key-note of the modern world.

### THE FOURTH DIMENSION

To express our sense of all this Newness many phrases have been invented. Of these the *Fourth Dimension* has obtained a currency quite outside the domain of mathematics, where it originated, and is frequently used as a synonym for what is new and strange.

He is therefore instructed to advance by the seven steps of wisdom. The symbolic meaning of these is probably well known to the Fratres. We may now regard them as referring to the seven liberal Arts and Sciences, but every step brings the Candidate nearer to the Altar and its Symbols, reminding him that:—

> "Thine are the forge, the loom, the mart,
> The wealth of land and sea;
> The world of Science and of Art
> Revealed and ruled by Thee."

One may, however, pause to consider one point in this particular part of the ceremony. The Candidate is led by the seven steps of wisdom to the "Symbolic centre of the Earth." He is instructed to stand on this centre with his arms extended, and he expresses his desire to approach the radiant East and to rejoice in the Light of Perfection. The question arises, how can the Candidate, standing where he does, ascertain the points of the compass, for to him there is no North, South, East, or West. The suggestion, therefore, is that this is a survival of the time when the theory that the Earth was flat found universal acceptance.

The secrets are now communicated, and it is worthy of notice that the Celebrant approaches from the radiant East.

"What inducement had you to leave the East and go to the West?"

"To seek for that which was lost, which by your instruction and our own industry we hope to find."

All that the search in the West can give is "substituted secrets." To find the genuine, we must return again to the source of light, to the Altar in the East, where alone we can find the key to a knowledge of the Divine which is the Aim and End of our quest, the attainment of which was seen in a vision by St. John-the-Divine, a portion of whose Revelation is now read by the Exponent (Rev. vii. 9-12).

Then is given a lecture on the symbolism of numbers, which as now given, indicates to the Candidate lines of study full of interest.

The symbolism of the burning of the M.T. is a fitting ending to a ceremony full of teaching, of interest and of value:—

> "So shall your light be extinguished from among us if you fail"

even as the flourishing vine of the Psalmist was burnt with fire and cut down (Ps. lxxx. 15). I conclude with the words of Dante:—

> "O Splendour of God whereby I saw the lofty triumph of the truthful realm—give me the power to tell how I beheld it."

The grand Pantheistic ideal, of the unknown and unknowable Essence being transformed first into subjective, and then into objective matter, is at the root of all these triads and triplets. Thus we find in philosophical Northern Buddhism (1) Âdi-Buddha (or Primordial Universal Wisdom) ; (2) the Dyhâni-Buddhas (or Bodhisattvas) ; (3) the Mânushi (Human) Buddhas. In European conceptions we find the same: God, Angels and Humanity symbolized theologically by the God-Man. The Brahmanical *Trimûrti* and also the three-fold body of Shiva, in Shaivism, have both been conceived on the same basis, if not altogether running on the lines of Esoteric teachings. Hence, no wonder if one finds this conception of the triple body—or the vestures of Nirmânakâya, Sambhogakâya and Dharmakâya, the grandest of the doctrines of Esoteric Philosophy—accepted in a more or less disfigured form by every religious sect, and explained quite incorrectly by the Orientalists. Thus, in its general application, the three-fold body symbolizes Buddha’s statue, his teachings and his stûpas ; in the priestly conceptions it applies to the Buddhist profession of faith called the *Triratna*, which is the formula of taking “refuge in Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha”. Popular fancy makes Buddha ubiquitous, placing him thereby on a par with an anthropomorphic god, and lowering him to the level of a tribal deity ; and, as a result, it falls into flat contradictions, as in Tibet and China. Thus the exoteric doctrine seems to teach that while in his Nirmânakâya body (which passed through 100,000 *kotis* of transformations on earth), he, Buddha, is at the same time a Lochana (a heavenly Dhyâni-Bodhisattva), in his Sambhogakâya “robe of absolute completeness”, and in Dhyâna, or a state which must cut him off from the world and all its connections; and finally and lastly he is, besides being a Nirmânakâya and a Sambhogakâya, also a Dharmakâya “of absolute purity”, a Vairotchana or Dhyâni-Buddha in full Nirvâna ! (See Eitel’s *Sanskrit-Chinese Dictionary*.) This is the jumble of contradictions, impossible to reconcile, which is given out by missionaries and certain Orientalists as the *philosophical* dogmas of Northern Buddhism. If not an intentional confusion of a philosophy dreaded by the upholders of a religion based in inextricable contradictions and guarded “mysteries”, then it is the product of ignorance. As the Trailokya, the Trikâya, and the Triratna are the three aspects of the same conceptions, and have to be, so to say, blended in one, the subject is further explained under each of these terms. (See also in this relation the term “Tri-sharana”.)

heretic, called Rokutsuponji, a reader of auguries, cunning in astrology and in the healing art. It happened, one day, that this heretic, being in company with Buddha, entered a forest, which was full of dead men’s skulls. Buddha, taking up one of the skulls and tapping it thus” (here the preacher tapped the reading-desk with his fan), “said, ‘What manner of man was this bone when alive?—and, now that he is dead, in what part of the world has he been born again?’ The heretic auguring from the sound which the skull, when struck, gave forth, began to tell its past history, and to prophesy the future. Then Buddha, tapping another skull, again asked the same questions. The heretic answered—

“‘Verily, as to this skull, whether it belonged to a man or a woman, whence its owner came or whither he has gone, I know not. What think you of it?’

“‘Ask me not,’ answered Buddha. But the heretic pressed him, and entreated him to answer; then Buddha said, ‘Verily this is the skull of one of my disciples, who forsook the lusts of the flesh.’

“Then the heretic wondered, and said—

“‘Of a truth, this is a thing the like of which no man has yet seen. Here am I, who know the manner of the life and of the death even of the ants that creep. Verily, I thought that no thing could escape my ken; yet here lies one of your disciples, than whom there lives no nobler thing, and I am at fault. From this day forth I will enter your sect, praying only that I may receive your teaching.’

“Thus did this learned heretic become a disciple of Buddha. If such an one as he was converted, how much the more should after-ages of ordinary men feel that it is through Buddha alone that they can hope to overcome the sinful lusts of the flesh! These lusts are the desires which agitate our hearts: if we are free from these desires, our hearts will be bright and pure; and there is nothing, save the teaching of Buddha, which can ensure us this freedom. Following the commands of Buddha, and delivered by him from our desires, we may pass our lives in peace and happiness.”

“‘Do not ask me,’ answered Buddha. But the heretic pressed him and begged him to answer; then Buddha said, ‘Truly, this is the skull of one of my disciples, who renounced the desires of the flesh.’

“Then the heretic wondered, and said—

“‘In truth, this is a thing the like of which no man has yet seen. Here am I, who know the way of the life and of the death even of the ants that creep. Truly, I thought that nothing could escape my knowledge; yet here lies one of your disciples, compared to whom no nobler being lives, and I am at fault. From this day forward I will enter your sect, praying only that I may receive your teaching.’

“Thus did this learned heretic become a disciple of Buddha. If even someone like him was converted, how much more should future generations of ordinary men feel that it is through Buddha alone that they can hope to overcome the sinful desires of the flesh! These desires are the passions which disturb our hearts: if we are free from these desires, our hearts will be bright and pure; and there is nothing, except the teaching of Buddha, which can ensure us this freedom. Following the commands of Buddha, and delivered by him from our desires, we may pass our lives in peace and happiness.”

translation:
14 ON THE THEOLOGY BOOK I.

It is perfectly proper that discourses respecting the Gods should be pure from physical investigations. For a mixture of this kind is, he says, laborious; and to make physical passions the end of mythological conjecture is the employment of no very good man—such as, for instance, a man who, through his [pretended] wisdom, considers the Chimera, the Gorgon, and things of a similar kind, as the same with physical phenomena. Socrates, in the Phaedrus, reprobating this mode of mythologizing, represents its patrons as saying, under the guise of a fable, that Orithyia, sporting with the wind Boreas and being thrown down the rocks, means nothing more than that Orithyia, who was a mortal, was ravished by Boreas through love. For it appears to me that fabulous narrations about the Gods should always have their concealed meaning more venerable than the apparent one. So that if certain persons introduce to us physical hypotheses of Platonic fables—such as are concerned with sublunary affairs—we must say that they entirely wander from the intention of the philosopher, and that those hypotheses alone are interpreters of the truth contained in these fables which have for their scope a divine, immaterial, and separate hypostasis, and which, looking to this, make the compositions and analyses of the fables adapted to our inherent anticipations of divine concerns.

---

CHAPTER V.

As we have therefore enumerated all these modes of the Platonic theology, and have shown what compositions and analyses of fables are adapted to the truth respecting the Gods, let us consider, in the next place, whence, and from what dialogues principally, we think the dogmas of Plato concerning the Gods may be collected, and by a speculation of what types or forms we may be able to distinguish his genuine writings from those spurious compositions which are ascribed to him.

The truth then concerning the Gods pervades, as I may say, through <note>For <term>oikeiais</term> (original: οἰκείαις), it is necessary to read <term>ousias</term> (original: οἰσίας).</note>

<summary>Proclus argues that Platonic myths should be interpreted as referring to divine, immaterial realities rather than physical, sublunary phenomena.</summary>

### The Eighteenth Chapter.

...to preserve the quality of the image, to live within it, or to fall out of it; that is, to turn to the right or to the left.

The eternal, effortless <note>original: "wirckloſe." In this mystical context, it suggests a state of pure, undisturbed potentiality or "being" that acts without the labor or struggle associated with created things.</note>, self-sufficient, endless, true, uncreated, unborn Being or Good, has born from itself another Being out of its own essence, in order to reveal itself therein—and through it and with it—and to call all things into being, whether they be invisible or visible. This born Being, because it does not exist of itself and is not its own essence (unlike the unborn Being), is rightly called an Image, a Son, a Radiance, or a Reflection of the Divine Majesty; a Word, Arm, Will, or Law of **GOD**. 

For in this [Being], the eternal and unborn allows itself to be contemplated and seen face to face, as in an image and a mirror. Through and with this, **GOD** creates, works, and governs all things, as if by His arm, hand, or tool; through it, He judges all creatures, etc. Such an image of the unborn Highest Good is called the firstborn before all creatures, because **God** has born all things through him into image and likeness—especially the angel and the human, the rational, free-willed creature. 

Now it is decreed in eternity: whoever is not found to be conformed to this Firstborn, and does not remain one with him, shall be cast out from the Heavenly Paradise. This Firstborn is the Word of **GOD**, the Will and Law of **GOD**, the true Image of the eternal and invisible God. Within this, the creature should live; that is, it should keep and preserve the nature, kind, and quality of an image. Namely, it should not belong to itself, for it is not from itself; it should not seek nor love itself, but rather Him whose image it bears. It should not claim for itself anything that is called or named good; it should not take ownership of the will, but rather leave it free

<margin>The character and nature of true faith.</margin>
Once you understand the nature and character of justifying faith and what Holy Scripture says about it—such as how it unites us with God; how it purifies hearts (Acts 15); how it overcomes the world (1 John 5); how it makes a new man out of the old (1 John 5); how it brings peace to the conscience (Romans 5), makes us righteous, and much more—then you will also be able to answer your fourth question for yourselves. dies, daß das gesellschaftliche Eigenthum sich auf die Erde und die andern Produktionsmittel erstreckt und das individuelle Eigenthum auf die übrigen Produkte, also auf die Verbrauchsgegenstände. Und damit die Sache auch für Kinder von sechs Jahren faßlich werde, unterstellt Marx auf Seite 56 einen „Verein freier Menschen, die mit gemeinschaftlichen Produktionsmitteln arbeiten und ihre individuellen Arbeitskräfte selbstbewußt als eine gesellschaftliche Arbeitskraft verausgaben,“ also einen sozialistisch organisirten Verein, und sagt: „Das Gesammtprodukt des Vereins ist ein gesellschaftliches Produkt. Ein Theil dieses Produkts dient wieder als Produktionsmittel. Er bleibt gesellschaftlich. Aber ein anderer Theil wird als Lebensmittel von den Vereinsmitgliedern verzehrt. Er muß daher unter sie vertheilt werden.“ Und das ist doch wohl klar genug, selbst für den verhegelten Kopf des Hrn. Dühring.

Das zugleich individuelle und gesellschaftliche Eigenthum, diese konfuse Zwittergestalt, diese bei der Hegeldialektik herauskommen müssende Ungereimtheit, diese Nebelwelt, dies tiefsinnige dialektische Räthsel, das Marx seinen Adepten zu lösen überläßt, — es ist abermals eine freie Schöpfung und Imagination des Herrn Dühring. Marx, als angeblicher Hegelianer ist verpflichtet, als Resultat der Negation der Negation eine richtige höhere Einheit zu liefern, und da er dies nicht nach dem Geschmack des Herrn Dühring thut, so muß dieser wiederum in höhern und edlern Styl verfallen, und Marx im Interesse der vollen Wahrheit Dinge unterschieben, die Herrn Dühring’s eigenstes Fabrikat sind. Ein Mann, der so total unfähig ist, auch nur ausnahmsweise richtig zu citiren, mag wohl in sittliche Entrüstung gerathen gegenüber der „Chinesengelehrsamkeit“ anderer Leute, die ausnahmslos richtig citiren, aber eben dadurch „den Mangel einer Einsicht in das Ideenganze der jedesmal angeführten Schriftsteller schlecht verdecken.“ Herr Dühring hat Recht. Es lebe die Geschichtszeichnung großen Styls!

Bisher sind wir von der Voraussetzung ausgegangen, Herrn Dühring’s hartnäckiges Falschcitiren sei wenigstens in gutem Glauben geschehen und beruhe entweder auf einer ihm eigenen totalen Unfähigkeit des Verständnisses, oder aber auf einer, der Geschichtszeichnung großen Stils eigenthümlichen und sonst wohl als liederlich bezeichneten Gewohnheit, aus dem Gedächt-

<vocab>Karl Marx, Eugen Dühring, Hegelianismus, Dialektik, Produktionsmittel, Eigenthum, Sozialismus, Zitierweise</vocab>
translation:
— 122 —

that social property extends to the earth and the other means of production, and individual property to the remaining products—that is, to the objects of consumption. And so that the matter might be graspable even for children of six years, Marx assumes on page 56 an "association of free men, who work with common means of production and consciously expend their individual labor-powers as a single social labor-power," that is, a socialistically organized association, and says: "The total product of the association is a social product. One portion of this product serves again as means of production. It remains social. But another portion is consumed by the members of the association as means of subsistence. It must therefore be distributed among them." And that is certainly clear enough, even for the "Hegelianized" head of Mr. Dühring.

The "simultaneously individual and social property," this confused hermaphroditic shape, this absurdity that must allegedly emerge from Hegelian dialectics, this fog-world, this profound dialectical riddle which Marx leaves his adepts to solve—it is once again a free creation and imagination of Mr. Dühring. Marx, as an alleged Hegelian, is obliged to provide a proper "higher unity" as the result of the negation of the negation, and since he does not do this to Mr. Dühring's taste, the latter must again fall into a "higher and nobler style" and, in the interest of "full truth," foist upon Marx things that are Mr. Dühring’s own manufacture. A man who is so totally incapable of quoting correctly, even by way of exception, may well fall into moral indignation toward the "Chinese erudition" of other people, who quote correctly without exception but who, by this very fact, "badly cover up the lack of an insight into the whole of the ideas of the writers cited in each case." Mr. Dühring is right. Long live the writing of history in the "grand style"!

Until now, we have proceeded from the assumption that Mr. Dühring’s stubborn misquoting happened at least in good faith and rested either on a total inability to understand, which is characteristic of him, or on a habit peculiar to the writing of history in the "grand style"—and otherwise usually termed sloppy—of quoting from memory.

translation: In the same way, after swaddling the other arm, let her continue to wrap the chest circumferentially with the wider bands, pressing the <term>endoein</term> <gloss>genital/pubic area</gloss> evenly in males, but tightening more firmly around the breasts in females, while loosening around the loin, for this shape is more appropriate for women. After these things, swaddle each of the legs individually. For to bind them together while they are bare is productive of ulceration, as the juxtaposition of tender surfaces with heat quickly causes sores. Furthermore, carry these wrappings of the bands down to the tips of the toes, loosening them around the thighs and the calves, but tightening them at the knees and the hams, and at the tarsi and the ankles, so that the ends of the feet are broadened and the middle parts are drawn together. After this, placing the arms against the sides and the feet against each other with a wide band, wrap the entire infant circumferentially from the chest down to the feet. For when the hands are positioned inside the wrapping, they become accustomed to extension, as the connections of the nerves that extend to the joints for a long time are thickening, so as to even bring about stiffness; however, by being wrapped, the hands are prevented from being distorted by irregular movement. Often, too, by bringing the fingers toward the eyes, the vision is harmed. Meanwhile, between the ankles and the knees, and also the elbows, wool should be placed so that the protuberances are not ulcerated by the overly forceful pressure and the juxtaposition of the parts.

### What is the analysis of syllogisms and how is it done.

Following these, [we come to] the analysis of syllogisms. As to what analysis might be, it is clear that it is the return from composite things to simple ones. Since, therefore, arguments are found in books, and these arguments are syllogisms, and it is necessary to analyze them completely, we come first to the head [to ask]: we shall seek the figure, under which figure the argument is brought. And it is clear that not every argument is concluded in the second [figure]—we shall seek if there is necessity—nor in the third, but in the first. Here there is nothing. In the first or in the second. But if someone [is] in the first and in the third, or through all [of them] and in the three. And the position of the middle term will guide us to this. For since in the first [figure], it is both subject and predicate; in the second, it is always a predicate; and in the third, it is always a subject. After this, we shall seek the propositions: which is the major, which is the minor, and the remaining one, along with those, we shall recognize and we shall add it. For often the writer omits this necessary one; at the same time, because [he might be] cutting some for the sake of brevity or grace, or he might wish to conceal everything, or he might prefer to clarify by way of induction. Therefore, it is necessary to know these things. And if we seek the necessary [proposition], for from the necessary and the propositions, the conclusion is made. Φοβουμένους δὲ τὴν Ἀσσυρίων δυναστείαν (τότε γὰρ ἐκείνους τῆς Ἀσίας κρατεῖν), ἐν τῇ νῦν Ἰουδαίᾳ καλουμένῃ πόλιν οἰκοδομησαμένους, τοσαύταις μυριάσιν ἀνθρώπων ἀρκέσουσαν, Ἱεροσόλυμα ταύτην ὀνομάσαι. » Τούτοις ἑξῆς τὴν διαδοχὴν τῶν κατ' Αἴγυπτον βασιλέων μετὰ τοῦ χρόνου τῆς ἀρχῆς αὐτῶν ἀπαριθμησάμενος, ἐπιλέγει· « Ταῦτα μὲν (18) ὁ Μάνεθως. Δῆλον δ' ἐστὶν, ἐκ τῶν εἰρημένων ἐτῶν τοῦ χρόνου συλλογισθέντος, ὅτι οἱ καλούμενοι ποιμένες, ἡμέτεροι δὲ πρόγονοι, τρισὶ καὶ ἐννενήκοντα καὶ τριακοσίοις πρόσθεν ἔτεσιν, ἐκ τῆς Αἰγύπτου ἀπαλλαγέντες, τὴν χώραν ταύτην ἀπῴκησαν (19), <margin>C</margin> ἢ Δαναὸν εἰς Ἄργος ἀφικέσθαι· καίτοι τοῦτον ἀρχαιότατον Ἀργεῖοι νομίζουσι. Δύο τοίνυν ὁ Μάνεθως ἡμῖν τὰ μέγιστα μεμαρτύρηκεν ἐκ τῶν παρὰ τοῖς Αἰγυπτίοις γραμμάτων· πρῶτον μὲν τὴν ἑτέρωθεν ἄφιξιν εἰς Αἴγυπτον, ἔπειτα δὲ τὴν ἐκεῖθεν ἀπαλλαγὴν, οὕτως ἀρχαίαν τοῖς χρόνοις ὡς ἐγγύς που προτερεῖν αὐτὴν τῶν Ἰλιακῶν ἔτεσι χιλίοις. » Ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν ἀπὸ τῆς Αἰγυπτιακῆς ἱστορίας ταύτῃ πῃ τῷ Ἰωσήπῳ κατὰ πλάτος ἀνιστόρηται· ἀπὸ δὲ τῆς Φοινίκων μάρτυσι χρησάμενος τοῖς τὰ Φοινικικὰ συγγραψαμένοις, παρίστησι τὸν ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις νεὼν ὑπὸ Σολομῶνος τοῦ βασιλέως ᾠκοδομῆσθαι ἔτεσι θᾶττον ἑκατὸν τεσσαράκοντα καὶ τρισὶ, καὶ μησὶν ὀκτὼ, τοῦ κτίσαι Τυρίους Καρχηδόνα. Εἶτα μεταβὰς, καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς περὶ Χαλδαίων ἱστορίας τὰς περὶ τῆς Ἑβραίων ἀρχαιότητος παρατίθεται μαρτυρίας.
