translation:
<meta>This page continues Eusebius’s presentation of evidence for the antiquity of the Hebrew people, specifically drawing on the Jewish historian Josephus, who in turn cites the Egyptian historian Manetho. The goal is to prove that the Hebrews (identified here with the "Shepherd Kings" or Hyksos) predated the most ancient figures of Greek myth and history.</meta>

# THE WORKS OF EUSEBIUS OF CAESAREA, PART II — APOLOGETICS.

<margin>A</margin> ...that a great and long-lasting war broke out against them, led by the kings of the Thebaid and the rest of Egypt. He [Manetho] records that at last, under a certain king named Misphraguthosis <note>original Latin: "Misphraguthosis"; Josephus records "Halisphraguthosis"</note>, those "Shepherds" <note>A reference to the Hyksos, a group of foreign rulers in Egypt whom Josephus identifies with the ancestors of the Jews</note> were defeated and driven out of the rest of Egypt, but were confined to a single place which encompassed ten thousand acres. This place was called Avaris. The same writer says that the Shepherds surrounded this entire area with a massive, strong wall to keep all their property and spoils safe and secure. However, Thmuthosis <note>original Latin: "Thmuthosin"; Josephus calls him "Thoumosis" or "Tethmosis"</note>, the son of Misphraguthosis, besieged the walls with an army of four hundred and eighty thousand men. Though he attempted to take it by force, he eventually despaired of the siege and struck a deal with them: they were to leave Egypt and go wherever they wished, entirely unharmed. Consequently, they departed Egypt with their entire families and all their possessions—numbering no fewer than two hundred and forty thousand people—and traveled through the desert toward Syria. Because they feared the power of the Assyrians (who then ruled over Asia), they built a city in the region we now call Judea, large enough to hold so many thousands of people, and they named it Jerusalem. After Manetho listed the succession of Egyptian kings and the length of their reigns, he concluded as follows: "Therefore, if we calculate the time according to these years, it is entirely clear that those whom they called 'Shepherds'—our ancestors—left Egypt and settled in that region three hundred and ninety-three years <margin>C</margin> before Danaus came to Argos, even though Danaus is celebrated by the Greeks as being of the highest antiquity." <margin>502</margin> Thus, two primary points are established by this testimony from Manetho, which follows the authority of Egyptian records: first, that these people came into Egypt from elsewhere; and second, that their departure from there was so ancient that it preceded the Trojan times by nearly a thousand years. Josephus recounts these matters from Egyptian history in some detail. He also demonstrates from Phoenician history, citing the Phoenician historians themselves, that the Temple of Jerusalem was built by King Solomon one hundred and forty-three years and eight months before the Tyrians founded Carthage. Then, moving on to the Chaldeans, he retrieves further evidence for the antiquity of the Hebrews from their monuments as well.

### CHAPTER XIV.
#### That the history of the Hebrews is older than the era of the Greek philosophers.

<margin>D</margin> Indeed, why is it necessary to pile demonstration upon demonstration, when there is no one who loves the truth more than...

---

(15) **Misphraguthosis.** In Josephus: **Halisphraguthosis.**
(16) **Thmuthosis.** In Josephus: **Thoumosis**, whom on page 1041 he calls **Tethmosis**.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...that a great and long-lasting war broke out. Under a king named Misphraguthosis (15), he says the Shepherds were defeated and driven out of the rest of Egypt, but were shut up in a place with a circumference of ten thousand acres. <margin>from Josephus: Abaris</margin> Avaris <gloss>Abaris</gloss> was the name of the place. Manetho says that the Shepherds built a great and strong wall around this entire area so they could hold all their property and their plunder in a fortified place. But Thmuthosis (16), the son of Misphraguthosis, attempted to take them by force through a siege (17), stationing four hundred and eighty thousand soldiers around the walls. When he gave up on the siege, he made a treaty so that they would leave Egypt and go wherever they wanted, all of them unharmed. <margin>B</margin> According to these agreements, they traveled with their whole households and possessions—numbering no fewer than twenty-four myriads <note>One myriad equals 10,000; thus, 240,000 people</note>—from Egypt through the desert into Syria. But because they feared the dynasty of the Assyrians (for at that time they ruled Asia), they built a city in what is now called Judea, sufficient for so many myriads of people, and named it Jerusalem." After this, having enumerated the succession of the kings in Egypt along with the time of each reign, he adds: "These things (18) are from Manetho. It is clear, when the time is calculated from the years mentioned, that those called Shepherds—who are our ancestors—left Egypt and settled in this land three hundred and ninety-three years <margin>C</margin> before Danaus arrived in Argos; yet the Argives consider him to be most ancient. Therefore, Manetho has testified to two of the greatest things for us from the Egyptian writings: first, the arrival in Egypt from elsewhere, and second, the departure from there, which was so ancient in its timing that it predates the Trojan War by somewhere near a thousand years." These matters from Egyptian history are thus recounted at length by Josephus. Using the authors who wrote Phoenician history as witnesses, he shows that the temple in Jerusalem was built by King Solomon one hundred and forty-three years and eight months before the Tyrians founded Carthage. Then, moving on, he presents the evidence concerning the antiquity of the Hebrews from the history of the Chaldeans.

### CHAPTER XIV.
#### That the times of the philosophers among the Greeks happen to be more recent than all the history of the Hebrews.

<margin>D</margin> But what need is there to heap up a multitude of proofs for one who loves the truth and is not fond of strife, and who is satisfied with what has been said, which contains a diverse account of...

(18) **These things, etc.** See Josephus, page 1041.
(19) **Settled.** To be corrected from Josephus as "dwelled in" <note>original: "ἐπῴκησαν"</note>, unless you prefer "migrated into the region" <note>original: "εἰς τὴν χώραν... ἀπῴκησαν"</note>.

<summary>Eusebius uses Josephus's citations of the Egyptian historian Manetho to argue that the Hebrews (identified as the "Shepherds") left Egypt and founded Jerusalem long before the earliest Greek historical figures like Danaus or the Trojan War. He further synchronizes the building of Solomon's Temple with the founding of Carthage to establish a relative chronology.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the classification of human actions, moving from those done under external compulsion to those done through ignorance. It picks up from the previous page's discussion on whether internal passions like lust or anger can be considered involuntary, concluding that they are indeed voluntary because the agent is the moving cause.</meta>

## ON THE FACULTIES

...even unwillingly <note>original: "etiam inuitè"</note>. Likewise, we perform certain actions through ignorance <term>per inscientiam: acting because one lacks specific information about the circumstances</term> which, once done, bring about distress; these have been called "unwillingly done" actions, which are followed by pain once they have been perpetrated. Of those things which are done through ignorance, there are two species: one is the **non-voluntary** act <note>original: "non sponte factum"</note>, and the other is the **unwilling** act <note>original: "inuitè factum"</note>. Our present purpose is to speak only of that which is done unwillingly. 

For that which is done "non-voluntarily" is more closely related to the "voluntary" act, as it is of a mixed nature. If you look at the beginning of the act, it is done unwillingly; yet if you look at the end, it is done voluntarily. For although the act was undertaken unwillingly, the outcome makes it seem as though it were done voluntarily. Therefore, they define the unwilling act in this way: An act is done "unwillingly" when, in addition to not being undertaken by choice, it also brings pain and a cause for repentance.

Furthermore, it is one thing to do something *through* ignorance, and another to act *while* being ignorant. For if the cause of the ignorance was within our own power, we are indeed acting while ignorant, yet not *through* ignorance. For instance, if a man who is full of wine <note>i.e., a drunkard</note> or someone who is enraged performs a wicked act, the one has drunkenness and the other has anger as the cause of their actions. These states were undertaken voluntarily, for it was within the man's power not to become drunk. 

He himself is therefore the cause of his own ignorance. Thus, he is not said to act *through* ignorance, but rather to act *while* ignorant; such actions are not involuntary, but voluntary. For this reason, those who act in this way are even rebuked by good men. For if he had not become drunk, he would not have committed the act; but since he became drunk voluntarily, he acted voluntarily. 

On the other hand, we act *through* ignorance when we ourselves have not provided the cause for that ignorance, but rather chance has brought it about: as when someone, shooting an arrow in a customary practice field, accidentally kills his father who was passing by at that moment. 

From these points we have discussed, it is demonstrated that the person who is ignorant of what is useful, or who believes that evil things are good, does not act unwillingly. For that brand of ignorance <term>inscientia: here used as a moral blindness rather than a lack of facts</term> arises from his own wickedness <note>original: "improbitas"</note>. Therefore, such a person is blamed. Furthermore, blame is not...

rather to His Majesty, who placed it in the hands of Monsieur de Villeroy <note>Nicolas de Neufville, Seigneur de Villeroy (1542–1617), a principal Secretary of State.</note> to make a report on it to him; at which everyone had cause to remain silent. From that moment, the King even began to soften his stance toward Monsieur du Plessis and recommended that he be better treated in his private affairs. This was perhaps due to the shock of such an atrocious proceeding <note>referring to the assassination plot</note>, or perhaps because of the distress he felt over the Conspiracy of Marshal de Biron, which he was discovering day by day, and against which he judged that Du Plessis's service could be useful to him. Thus, when His Majesty came to Blois in the month of May, Monsieur du Plessis was advised, after such a display of royal indignation, to withdraw further away. This he would not do, being assured of his innocence and committing himself entirely to the providence of God. And indeed, His Majesty told Monsieur de Villeroy that if Du Plessis came to find him, he would receive him warmly; he even told Monsieur de Loménie <note>Antoine de Loménie, another of the King's secretaries of state.</note> that he wanted him to travel down to Saumur to see Du Plessis on his behalf. 

But Monsieur de Rosny <note>Maximilien de Béthune, Duke of Sully, a powerful minister and Du Plessis's nephew by marriage.</note>—whether he wished to have the credit for reconciling him with the King, or whether he wished to avert this meeting entirely—told His Majesty that at the first opportunity he would go see him himself with his wife, the niece of Monsieur du Plessis, and that he owed him this service. He later excused this by the haste of his return; and thus Monsieur du Plessis saw neither the one nor the other. This was, in truth, according to his own wish; because, being resolved to publish his *Response to the Bishop of Évreux* <note>Jacques Davy du Perron, the Bishop of Évreux, who had "defeated" Du Plessis in the famous 1600 Fontainebleau debate regarding alleged false citations in Du Plessis's book on the Eucharist.</note> which was then ready, he feared that as a price for returning to His Majesty’s good graces, they might impose a condition that he write no more. This he could not accept in good conscience, nor could he refuse it without offending the King. But His Majesty having turned his path toward Paris, Monsieur du Plessis sent Monsieur Marbaut, his secretary, to erase his fault—if any were found—with letters dated June 2nd in these words:

> *SIRE, the last look I had the misfortune of receiving from Your Majesty has made me apprehensive about presenting myself before you, not being sufficiently assured of your good graces. Not, however, that I have not glimpsed through my darkness some sparks of your goodness toward me; but they were so quickly extinguished that they served to dazzle rather than enlighten me; so little followed by action that I felt I must restrain myself in a doubtful reverence, rather than allow myself a presumptuous confidence. I therefore have recourse, SIRE, to most humbly beseeching Your Majesty to forgive me either for this justified fear or this hesitant respect; and nevertheless to remember the fidelity of my years passed,*

The rich man awakes from his sleep; and he finds nothing in his hands of the treasures he had dreamt of. On another side, it <note>The "Wisdom of the Cross" mentioned on the previous page.</note> places before our eyes a voluptuary <note>A person devoted to luxury and sensual pleasures.</note>, who has consumed his wealth and his health in fine dining and in other pleasures, which modesty forbids naming: Here he is, nailed to a bed, or to an armchair by the gout, which his debauches <note>Historical term for excessive indulgence in physical pleasures, which was commonly believed to cause ailments like gout.</note> have brought upon him: What has become of his pleasures? They have become for him a continual torment and a painful repentance: as many pleasures, so many torments; where one has sinned, there one is punished. But the man sensitive to the ills of the body remains almost always insensitive to the ills of the soul; until finally his time passes, and God's time comes after this life: it is then that one will pay dearly <note>Original: "payera la folle enchere." Literally "to pay the foolish overbid," an idiom meaning to suffer the heavy consequences of one's reckless choices.</note>, and one will read the chapter on Crosses after death.

108      THE WAY

whatever the evils of which they complain.

<margin>Patiently enduring great evils.</margin> Let us place before our eyes the holy Hermits of past centuries <note>Teresa refers to the Desert Fathers and the early hermits of Mount Carmel, whom the Discalced Carmelites looked to as their spiritual ancestors.</note> whom we consider as our fathers, and whose life we claim to imitate. How many labors and pains did they suffer in their solitude from the extreme harshness of the cold, the excessive heat of the sun, hunger, and so many other discomforts, without having anyone to whom they could complain, except to God alone? Do you believe, then, that they were made of iron, and not of flesh and bone like us?

Be certain, my Daughters <note>original: "mes Filles"; Teresa’s affectionate term for the nuns in her care.</note>, that when we begin to conquer and discipline our bodies, they no longer torment us so much. There will be others enough who will take care of what is necessary for you; do not fear to forget yourselves, unless an evident necessity obliges you to remember it.

If we do not resolve to trample underfoot the fear of death and the loss of our health, we will never do anything of worth. Endeavor— <note>The text cuts off mid-word ("Effor-") and continues on the following page.</note>

<margin>Sauces.</margin>

### Sauffe à la Sultane.

Mettez dans une cafferole une chopine de bouillon avec un verre de vin blanc, deux tranches de citron, la peau ôtée, deux cloux de girofle, une gouffe d'ail, une demi-feuille de laurier, persil, ciboule, un oignon, & une racine; faites bouillir une heure & demie à petit feu & réduire au point d'une sauffe, passez-la au tamis, ensuite vous y mettrez un peu de sel, gros poivre, un jaune d'œuf dur haché, une pincée de persil blanchi haché très-fin.

### Sauffe à l'Allemande.

Mettez dans une cafferole un peu de coulis avec autant de bouillon, une pincée de persil blanchi haché, deux foyes de volailles cuits, un anchois & des câpres, le tout haché très-fin, gros comme la moitié d'un œuf de bon beurre, sel, gros poivre, faites lier la sauffe sur le feu, & vous en servez à ce que vous jugerez à propos.

### Sauffe à l'Angloise.

Hachez deux jaunes d'œufs durs, mettez-en la moitié dans une cafferole avec un anchois & des câpres hachées, un verre de bon bouillon, peu de sel, gros poivre; gros comme la moitié d'un œuf de beurre manié d'une pincée de farine, faites lier la sauffe sur le feu; dressez-la sur ce que vous voudrez, & jetterez sur la viande le restant du jaune d'œuf haché. Cette sauffe est bonne pour masquer des entrées qui manquent de bonne mine.

<header>THE BOURGEOIS COOK</header>

<margin>Sauces.</margin>

### Sultana Sauce.

Place in a saucepan a pint of broth with a glass of white wine, two slices of lemon with the peel removed, two cloves, a clove of garlic, half a bay leaf, parsley, scallions, an onion, and a root vegetable. Boil for an hour and a half over a low fire and reduce to the consistency of a sauce. Pass it through a sieve, then add a little salt, coarse pepper, a chopped hard-boiled egg yolk, and a pinch of very finely chopped blanched parsley.

### German Sauce.

Place in a saucepan a little <term>coulis</term> with an equal amount of broth, a pinch of chopped blanched parsley, two cooked poultry livers, an anchovy, and some capers, all chopped very finely. Add good butter the size of half an egg, salt, and coarse pepper. Bind the sauce over the fire and serve it as you see fit.

### English Sauce.

Chop two hard-boiled egg yolks. Place half in a saucepan with an anchovy and chopped capers, a glass of good broth, a little salt, and coarse pepper. Add butter the size of half an egg mixed with a pinch of flour. Bind the sauce over the fire. Arrange it over whatever you wish and scatter the remaining chopped egg yolk over the meat. This sauce is good for masking entrées that lack an appealing appearance.

Il capitello s'allontana molto da gli scritti di Vitruuio, perche egli è di maggiore altezza senza la cimasa, che non lo descriue Vitruuio con tutta la cimasa; et nondimeno per la comune opinione sono i più bei capitelli che siano in Ro-anco quei del portico; di maniera che io giudico, sì come da principio io dissi, non hauer trouato edificio fatto con maggiore osseruanza dell'ordine, quanto è questo: et s'io volessi scriuere tante belle osseruanze che vi sono, così dentro come di fuori, io parrei forse troppo prolisso; et perdì di questo marauiglioso edificio farò fine, seguitando dell'altre antichità.

translation:
### OF ANTIQUITIES

The four figures below here are members of the tabernacle beside this, as the letters A, B, C, D denote, which correspond approximately to the measurements of the heights stated here behind. But let it suffice for the Architect that all things, member by member, are diligently transported from the large ones and reduced to this form proportionally. And although perhaps to the students of <term>Vitruvius</term> this cornice will seem too high in proportion to the architrave and the frieze—and I for my part would not make it so high—nevertheless, seeing it in that place which has great distance and is not very high, it represents good proportion. The capital departs much from the writings of <term>Vitruvius</term>, because it is of greater height without the <term>cimasa</term> <gloss>crown molding/cymatium</gloss> than <term>Vitruvius</term> describes it with the entire <term>cimasa</term>. And nevertheless, by common opinion, they are the most beautiful capitals that exist in Rome, as are those of the portico. In such a way that I judge, just as I said from the beginning, that I have not found an edifice made with greater observance of the order than this is. And if I wanted to write of all the beautiful observances that are there, both inside and out, I would perhaps seem too prolix. And so, I will make an end of this marvelous building, continuing with other antiquities.

De wakk're **WILLEM**, Prins van 't wydberoemde Oranje,
Die Nederland verlofte, in wederwil van Spanje,
Van 't onverdraaglyk juk der slaafsche dwinglandy,
En uit de banden der Gewetenstiranny.
De wetenschappen zyn in uwen kreits herboren.
Gamaliëls doen zich in u geduurig hooren,
En teelen, niet alleen voor Kerk, en Stad en Staat,
Maar voor al de Aarde een reeks van Mannen, vroeg en laat;
Van Mannen, die uw roem hoe langs hoe meer doen groeijen.
Steeds moet ge, ô Hooge School! door Letterhelden bloeijen,
Wier lof de lof verdooft, gelyk zy altoos deed,
Van al wat ooit zyn vlyt den Lett'ren heeft besteed.
Nu lust het my de **KERK VAN PIETER** te bekyken.
Dit Kerkgesticht behoeft in schoonheid niet te wyken
Voor een gebouw waar mede een Stad in Holland praalt.
Zyn pracht en luister, daar 't nieuwsgierig oog in dwaalt,
Bekoort me! langen tyd moet het zyn stant behouwen.
De **KERK VAN 'T HOOGELAND**, een uwer Hoofdgebouwen
ô Leyden! dryft me voort: Daar zie ik 't fraai gesticht,
Dat voor vier eeuwen kwam zo heerlyk in het licht!
Zyn luister, zwier en stant kan mynen geest behaagen.
De **LIEVEVROUWE KERK**, die laater op kwam dagen,
En kleener is, behoeft in netheid en sieraad,
Ook niet te zwichten voor een Kerk van Neêrlands Staat.
Ik ga naar 't **GASTHUIS** toe, genaamd na Sint **KATRYNE**:
Hier word den zieken, moede en afgemat door pyne,
Verkwikt, gekoestert en geneezen en hersteld;
En hem, die d' Armoede in zyn banden houd beknelt,
Word hier verzadigt, en voorzien met dak en kleeren,
Terwyl de Kerk hen dient, om 't waare woord des Heeren
Te hooren, op dat dus de ziel, zo min als 't lyf,
Haar voedzel derve, en niet om troost verlegen blyf.
Steeds moet de liefde tot elks nut uw hart doen blaaken,
ô Leydsburgery! zo zal de Godheid waaken
Voor 't welzyn van uw Stad, en Godsdienst, als voorheen.
Nu eens 't **BEGGYNHOF** van de Maagden ingetreen,
Die, naar de Roomsche wyz', de Kerk, haar kuisheid weyden,
Of eer, uit Bygeloof, een eenzaam leeven leyden;
Zyn stant is lustig; en de **KERK**, die 't Hof verfiert,
Waar in de Godsdienst word, naar **ENG'LANDS** trant, geviert,
Is fraai en lovenswaard. Nu elders heen getreden.
Hier zie 'k de **KERK**, waarin, naar Duitsche taal en zeden,
De Godsdienst word geleerd. Wat verder zie ik 't gesticht
Der **NIEUWE KERK**, waarin, Gods heilwoord, naar het licht
Van 't Euangely word ontvouwt aan elks gedachten.
ô Heerlyk timmerwerk, om uwen stant hoog te achten!
Strek eeuwen lang 't cieraad van Leyden; dat zo trouw
Zyn tyd en vlyt en geld bestede aan uwen bouw.
Ik heb geen stof om van de **LOOTSKERKE** iets te reppen.
Nu 't my gebeuren mag myn adem weêr te scheppen

<meta>catchword: Op</meta>

<column-break/>

Op 't vlakke land, neem ik, ô Leyden! met deez' wensch
Van u myn afscheid: dat nooit tyd uw roem verlensch':
Uw welvaart groeije en bloeije, in wederwil der jaaren:
De Zon van uw geluk duik' nimmer in de baaren
Van druk noch tegenspoed; maar straale, al 't Land ten troost,
In ongestoorden loop uit een gezegent Oost.
Nu roept my 't **PESTHUIS**, dat, byna een eeuw geleden,
Gebouwt, door 't wyz' beleid van Leydens Overheden,
Niet weinig aanziens heeft. Hier worden, wen de dood,
Door 't Pestvuur, hevig woed, en dreigt met zwaaren nood
De Inboorelingen, hen een goed verblyf gegeeven,
Die in gevaar zyn om door zulk een kwaal te sneeven.
Nu strekt het ten verblyf van zieke en arme Liên.
Nooit moet ge, ô Leyden! aan dit Huis het onheil zien,
Dat laatst het Pesthuis moest van Amsteldam bezuuren;
't Geen in één nacht verbrand, alleenig zyne muuren
Voor 't vuur bewaaren zag. Doch treên we verder voort.
ô Heuglyk **TUINGEZICHT**, dat, by de **MAREPOORT**,
Langs Haarlems Trekvaart is te zien! gy streelt myn zinnen.
Wie can uw fraaiheid en vermaaklykheid ontginnen?
Myn veder is te zwak, en mynen geest te kleen.
Een ander **TUINGEZICHT** lokt my weêr elders heen,
Dat, **AAN DEN RHYN** zich koomt ontdekken aan myn oogen.
Hier ziet men Jachten, door den koelen wind bewoogen,
Spanfeeren langs uw rug, ô aangenaame stroom!
Dien vader Vondel achte als zynen zoetsten droom,
In 't onnavolgbaar dicht, zo schoon, zo onbedwongen,
En zielverrukkende tot uwen roem gezongen.
Maar noch veel fraayer toont ge, ô **RHYN**! u in 't verschiet,
Daar myn nieuwsgierig oog, u by de **ZYLBRUG** ziet.
ô Aangenaam vertoog! hoe streelt ge myn gedachten!
Wie moet uw fraaiheid niet verheffen en hoog achten?
Waar ik myn oogen wend of keer, ik zie ze blind;
't Zy ik den Hengelaar, die zyn genoegen vind,
Zo hy een vischje mag verschalken, koom beschouwen:
Het zy ik my vermaake in keurige Gebouwen
En Lustpriëelen, die den Tuinen tot sieraad
Verstrekken; of het zy ik de oogen vrolyk laat
Aen de een en d'and're kant van uwe boorden weyden;
Of 't zy 'k van ver begluur het schoon en fierlyk Leyden.
ô Lieflyk Rhyngezicht, en Lusttoonneel van weeld'!
Nooit hebt ge mynen geest met meer vermaak gestreelt.
Maar 'k moet met tegenzin my elders heen begeeven,
Terwyl gy eindloos zult in myn gedachten zweeven.
Het **HUIS TER MEY**, het welk een uwer Raaden hoord,
De Heer van **LANDSCHOT**, trekt me, ô Leyden! zagjes voort.
Hoe fraai vertoont het zich uit eenen reeks van boomen!
Wat is 't my een vermaak om u te wellekomen,
Wyl ik het honk haast zie van d'aangevange reis!
Maar wie verheft u, naar uw voeglykheid en eisch?

<meta>catchword: Dit</meta>

<vocab>Leyden, Willem van Oranje, Kerk van Pieter, Kerk van 't Hoogeland, Lievevrouwe Kerk, Gasthuis, Sint Katryne, Beggynhof, Nieuwe Kerk, Pesthuis, Rhyn, Zylbrug, Vondel, Tuingezicht</vocab>
translation:
The valiant **WILLIAM**, Prince of the widely famous Orange,
Who liberated the Netherlands, in spite of Spain,
From the unbearable yoke of slavish tyranny,
And from the bonds of the tyranny of conscience.
The sciences are reborn in your circle.
Gamaliels <note>A reference to the biblical teacher of Paul, signifying learned scholars or theologians.</note> make themselves heard in you constantly,
And raise, not only for Church, and City and State,
But for all the Earth a series of Men, early and late;
Of Men, who make your fame grow more and more.
Always must you, oh University! flourish through Men of Letters,
Whose praise dulls all other praise, as it always did,
Of all who ever devoted their diligence to Letters.
Now it pleases me to view the **CHURCH OF PETER** <note>Pieterskerk, a historic church in Leiden</note>.
This Church foundation need not yield in beauty
To any building with which a City in Holland boasts.
Its splendor and luster, in which the curious eye wanders,
Charms me! It must preserve its standing for a long time.
The **CHURCH OF THE HIGHLAND** <note>Hooglandse Kerk</note>, one of your Main Buildings
Oh Leyden! draws me forward: There I see the beautiful foundation,
That came so gloriously into the light four centuries ago!
Its luster, elegance, and standing can please my spirit.
The **LADY CHURCH** <note>Vrouwenkerk</note>, which appeared later,
And is smaller, does not need to yield in neatness and ornament
To any Church of the Dutch State.
I go toward the **HOSPITAL**, named after Saint **CATHERINE**:
Here the sick, weary and exhausted by pain,
Are refreshed, cherished, healed, and restored;
And he, whom Poverty holds gripped in its bonds,
Is satiated here, and provided with roof and clothing,
While the Church serves them, to hear the true word of the Lord,
So that the soul, as little as the body,
Lacks its nourishment, and remains not wanting for comfort.
Love for the benefit of each must always make your heart glow,
Oh people of Leiden! thus shall the Divinity watch
Over the welfare of your City, and Religion, as before.
Now once entered into the **BEGUINAGE** <note>Beggynhof, a residential court for pious women</note> of the Maidens,
Who, according to the Roman way, pasture the Church, their chastity,
Or formerly, out of Superstition, led a solitary life;
Its standing is pleasant; and the **CHURCH**, which adorns the Court,
In which Religion is celebrated according to the manner of **ENGLAND**,
Is beautiful and praiseworthy. Now stepped elsewhere.
Here I see the **CHURCH**, in which, according to German language and customs,
Religion is taught. Somewhat further I see the foundation
Of the **NEW CHURCH**, in which God's holy word is unfolded,
According to the light of the Gospel, to everyone's thoughts.
Oh glorious carpentry, highly to be esteemed for your standing!
Be for centuries long the ornament of Leyden, that so faithfully
Spent its time and diligence and money on your construction.
I have no material to mention anything of the **PILOT'S CHURCH**.
Now that it may happen to me to catch my breath again

<column-break/>

On the flat land, I take, oh Leyden! with this wish
My farewell from you: that time may never shorten your fame:
May your prosperity grow and flourish, in spite of the years:
May the Sun of your happiness never dive into the waves
Of pressure or adversity; but shine, for the comfort of the Land,
In an undisturbed course from a blessed East.
Now the **PEST HOUSE** <note>Pesthuis, a historic plague hospital</note> calls me, which, built almost a century ago,
Through the wise policy of the Authorities of Leyden,
Has no little appearance. Here, when death,
Through the Plague-fire, rages violently, and threatens with heavy need
The inhabitants, they are given a good residence,
Who are in danger of perishing through such an ailment.
Now it serves as a residence for sick and poor People.
Never must you, oh Leyden! see in this House the misfortune
That the Pest House of Amsterdam last had to suffer;
Which burned in one night, and saw only its walls
Preserved from the fire. But let us step further.
Oh memorable **GARDEN VIEW**, which, by the **MARE GATE** <note>Marepoort</note>,
Along the Haarlem Tow-path is to be seen! You caress my senses.
Who can mine your beauty and enjoyableness?
My quill is too weak, and my spirit too small.
Another **GARDEN VIEW** lures me elsewhere again,
Which, **BY THE RHINE**, comes to reveal itself to my eyes.
Here one sees Yachts, moved by the cool wind,
Running along your back, oh pleasant stream!
Which father Vondel <note>Joost van den Vondel, the most famous 17th-century Dutch poet</note> deemed his sweetest dream,
In the inimitable poem, so beautiful, so unforced,
And soul-ravishingly sung to your glory.
But even much more beautifully do you show yourself, oh **RHINE**! in the distance,
Where my curious eye sees you by the **ZYL BRIDGE**.
Oh pleasant demonstration! How you caress my thoughts!
Who must not exalt your beauty and esteem it highly?
Wherever I turn or twist my eyes, I see them blinded;
Whether I come to contemplate the Angler, who finds his pleasure,
If he may deceive a little fish;
Whether I amuse myself in elegant Buildings
And Pleasure-pavilions, that serve as ornament to the Gardens;
Or whether I let the eyes joyfully pasture
On the one and the other side of your banks;
Or whether I glimpse from afar the beautiful and proud Leyden.
Oh lovely Rhine-view, and Pleasure-scene of wealth!
Never have you caressed my spirit with more pleasure.
But I must reluctantly betake myself elsewhere,
While you will endlessly hover in my thoughts.
The **HOUSE TER MEY**, which belongs to one of your Councilors,
The Lord of **LANDSCHOT**, draws me, oh Leyden! softly forward.
How beautifully it presents itself from a series of trees!
What a pleasure it is for me to welcome you,
While I soon see the home of the begun journey!
But who elevates you, according to your appropriateness and demand?

<summary>The author continues their poetic tour of Leiden, describing its religious, charitable, and public institutions, before proceeding to the gardens and riverscapes along the Rhine.</summary>

<margin>See various old watchtowers along the beach.</margin>
Furthermore, one sees here along the beach various very old towers, and among others two special ones that have been renewed, in which the Druze keep watch in order to quickly discover pirates. But the others, of which there are still many standing along the beach, each a mile apart, have mostly fallen into decay due to age.

Some believe that they were built in the past by order of the Roman Emperors so that, if any people rebelled or a war arose suddenly, one would have news of it sooner in Constantinople. They gave the signal and sign by night with a bright flame of fire, and by day with heavy smoke, before the invention of the cannon; although even now, these signs are maintained here in place of cannon shots.

In the afternoon, when the wind had died down and our progress was therefore slow, we saw the small village of Carniola high up in the evening; and not long after that, below at the end of the high Lebanon mountains toward the south, the city of Sidon, still called <term>Seida</term> <gloss>local name for Sidon</gloss> by the inhabitants at this time. It is not particularly large, but in outward appearance, it is fairly well built and guarded by two castles, of which one lies on a high cliff toward the north and the other on a high hill. Those who wish to travel to Safed, a day's journey from here, dock here. Before we reached it, night overtook us with headwinds, which hindered us so much—

they went to their King's grandfather to request the pipes for the use of water at <term>Chapultepec</term>, located but a mile from <term>Mexico</term>. This was gladly granted to them. However, when they attempted to lead this water toward the city with very great difficulty, having made water-gutters from sods of earth and some piling which had to be laid across the lake, the gutters broke, so that the water became murky and undrinkable again. After this, <margin>Occasion for war given.</margin> they requested of the aforementioned King—though with harsher words, perhaps intentionally, in order to break with the <term>Tepanecas</term>—pretending that, since they could not enjoy the water because the water pipes were unusable, he should send them wood, lime, stone, and workmen so that they might construct a permanent water-conduit that would provide them with good water. The King, taking this overly commanding request ill, viewed it as an overly arrogant intention of **Subjects** against their **Sovereign**; and seeing himself bolstered by his councilors, he sent this answer back to them: "You, inhabitants of the land of reeds, what do you presume for yourselves? Soon one shall let you know what is to be thought of your conduct, thus you shall soon see your arrogance pruned." It was also immediately forbidden on pain of death, and publicly proclaimed, that no one should have any further dealings with the <term>Mexicans</term>, and even less should they enter their city, nor should they grant them any access to theirs. The King, likewise seeing that his council and citizenry were plotting to exterminate the <term>Mexicans</term>, requested that they first place the young King in his hands, as then they could settle matters with the <term>Mexicans</term> as they pleased. aan de Vorstenlandsche hoven, waar de traditie inzake den dans beter dan waar ook zich heeft gehandhaafd, worden de *kemanak* (afb. 68 op den voorgrond) uitsluitend geslagen ter begeleiding van de *bedaja-dansen* ¹).

Verder levert ook de omstandigheid, dat het zeven-tal *tjeloering* in den Djocja'schen kraton de pélogschaal draagt, een versterking voor mijne veronderstelling ²). Immers zoowel de *bedaja-dansen*, als die der *serimpi* en evenzoo het gewone *lajoeban*, worden uitgevoerd op *pélog*-muziek (waarbij de hoogst zeldzame uitzonderingen den regel bevestigen) ³). *Pélog* is het echte dans-toongeslacht, gelijk *sléndro* het *wayanggenus*.

Het bovenstaande was geschreven, toen de heer Heyting mij wees op het mogelijke verband — ook reeds door Van der Tuuk ⁴) gelegd — tusschen *tjeloering* (*celuring*) en het vrij dikwijls voorkomende ⁵) Hindoe-Javaansche *curing*. Dr. Goris was zoo vriendelijk, mij dit nader toe te lichten, door mede te deelen, dat het infix *el* een veelvuldigheid of een zich herhalen aanduidt; *celuring* zou dus beteekenen: veel *curing*, of ,,overal'' of ,,herhaaldelijk'' *curing*. translation:
in the courts of the Princely States, where the tradition regarding dance has been maintained better than anywhere else, the <term>kemanak</term> (fig. 68 in the foreground) are played exclusively to accompany the <term>bedaja</term> dances <note>1</note>.

Furthermore, the circumstance that the set of seven <term>tjeloering</term> in the Djocja court carries the <term>pélog</term> scale also provides reinforcement for my supposition <note>2</note>. Indeed, both the <term>bedaja</term> dances and those of the <term>serimpi</term>, as well as the ordinary <term>lajoeban</term>, are performed to <term>pélog</term> music (with the highly rare exceptions proving the rule) <note>3</note>. <term>Pélog</term> is the true dance tone-gender, just as <term>sléndro</term> is the <term>wayang</term> genus.

-><gloss>In musical scores, written as "Rising"</gloss><- <note>original: 卬 (*ang*). This abbreviated character is the standard shorthand used in Guqin tablature to represent the *Yi* (抑) technique.</note>

<note>The metaphor of the **Swallow Chasing Flying Insects** (*Yan zhu fei chong shi*) captures the agile and predatory precision required for this movement. Just as a swallow must be both swift and remarkably accurate to catch a flying insect mid-air, the musician’s fingers must maintain a firm, constant pressure (*Yi*) against the string while moving rapidly between positions. This ensures that the "voice" of the instrument does not flicker or fade during the slide.</note>

<term>Left Hand: Thumb, Middle, and Ring Fingers (大中名指): These are the primary fingers used for "stopping" the strings on the Guqin. The thumb (Great finger), middle, and ring (Nameless) fingers each have specific points of contact with the string to produce different tonal qualities.</term>

<note>The illustration on this page (noted in the original manuscript) depicts a hand with fingers extended elegantly, positioned above a swallow in flight. This visual aid served as a mnemonic for students to remember the combination of physical lightness in the arm and firm "weightedness" in the fingertips.</note>

# Treatise on Armament Technology, Volume 101

### Military Equipment: Warfare — Banners and Flags, Part 3

The **Squad Leader’s identifying flag** is one square foot in size. The pole used for this flag is a **long spear**, fifteen feet in length. The flag itself is to be suspended at a height of nine feet from the ground.
<note>original: 隊長認旗方一尺桿用長鎗一丈五尺旗懸高九尺. In the Ming military system popularized by General Qi Jiguang, the "long spear" served as both a primary weapon and a mobile flagpole, ensuring the squad leader could lead the charge while remaining a visible point of alignment for his twelve men.</note>

The total weight is two catties.
<note>original: 重二斤 (zhòng èr jīn). A "catty" or jin during the Ming period was approximately 590 grams, making the entire assembly roughly 1.2 kilograms or 2.6 pounds.</note>

<term>Squad Leader<note>original: 隊長 (duìzhǎng). The leader of a *duì*, the smallest tactical unit. In the "Mandarin Duck Formation," this leader stood at the front, directing the combined efforts of spearmen, shield-bearers, and branch-wielders.</note></term>

<term>Identifying Flag<note>original: 認旗 (rènqí). Also known as "recognition flags," these allowed soldiers to identify their specific unit and leader amidst the smoke and chaos of the battlefield.</note></term>

# Monthly Solitude and Void Positions
<note>In traditional Chinese metaphysics and military theory, "Solitude" (Gu) and "Void" (Xu) are paired opposites used to determine favorable directions. "Solitude" represents a concentrated, singular force of energy, while "Void" represents emptiness or vulnerability. A common strategic maxim was to "occupy the Solitude and strike the Void."</note>

| Month | Location of Solitude | Location of the Void |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Second Month | Solitude is at **Gen**, in the Northeast <term>Gen (艮): The trigram representing the Mountain and the Northeast direction.</term> | Void is in the Southwest |
| Third Month | Solitude is at **Zhen**, in the True East <term>Zhen (震): The trigram representing Thunder and the East direction.</term> | Void is in the True West |
| Fourth Month | Solitude is at **Xun**, in the Southeast <term>Xun (巽): The trigram representing Wind and the Southeast direction.</term> | Void is in the Northwest |
| Fifth Month | Solitude is at **Xun**, in the Southeast | Void is in the Northwest |
| Sixth Month | Solitude is at **Li**, in the True South <term>Li (離): The trigram representing Fire and the South direction.</term> | Void is in the True North |
| Seventh Month | Solitude is at **Kun**, in the Southwest <term>Kun (坤): The trigram representing the Earth and the Southwest direction.</term> | Void is in the Northeast |
| Eighth Month | Solitude is at **Kun**, in the Southwest | Void is in the Northeast |
| Ninth Month | Solitude is at **Dui**, in the True West <term>Dui (兌): The trigram representing the Lake and the West direction.</term> | Void is in the True East |
| Tenth Month | Solitude is at **Qian**, in the Northwest <term>Qian (乾): The trigram representing Heaven and the Northwest direction.</term> | Void is in the Southeast |

<note>Notice that the positions of Solitude and Void are always direct opposites on the compass. For example, in the Second Month, Solitude is Northeast while the Void is Southwest. Some months, such as the Fourth and Fifth, or the Seventh and Eighth, share the same directional alignments.</note>

<summary>This page provides a reference table for "Monthly Solitude and Void" positions, mapping lunar months to specific compass directions and trigrams. It is used to determine advantageous directions for movement or action during specific times of the year.</summary>

**Verse:** By applying half of the fast-result <note>original: "shighraphala"</note> to the planet’s position, the planet is prepared. Then, by adjusting for the slow-apogee <note>original: "mandocca"</note> and applying the slow-result, the planet becomes "Slow-True." Finally, by applying the full fast-result, the planet's daily true position is established.

**Meaning:** The method is as follows: From the fast-center <term>Shighra-kendra: The angular distance of the planet from its fast anomaly point</term>, calculate the fast-result. Take half of this value and apply it (add or subtract) to the mean planet. Following this, calculate the slow-apogee <term>Mandochcha: The point of the planet's slowest motion, similar to the aphelion</term> and apply half of the resulting slow-correction. Then, re-calculate the slow-apogee to find the full slow-result; apply this full result to the original mean planet to obtain the "Slow-True" planet <note>original: "Mandasphuta"</note>. If you then subtract this Slow-True position from the planet's own fast-motion point to find the fast-center, and apply that full fast-result to the Slow-True planet, you will arrive at the final "True" positions of the planets.

### Calculating the True Slow-Velocity

**Verse:** Multiply the Sine-segment <note>original: "jyakhanda"</note> produced by the slow-center by the planet's daily motion. Divide the result by 225. Then, multiply by the multiplier and divide by 80 <note>original: "khnu-nagai"</note> to find the correction for the velocity.

**Meaning:** Take the difference of the Sines <term>Jyakhanda: The difference between consecutive entries in a Sine table</term> of the slow-center and multiply it by the specific planetary velocity. Divide this product by 225. Take the resulting value and multiply it by the slow-circumference multipliers, then divide by 80. The result will be in seconds of arc <note>original: "vliptas"</note>; divide this by 60 to convert it into minutes of arc <note>original: "kalas"</note>. This result is the velocity-correction <note>original: "gati-phala"</note>. If the center is in the first or last quadrants, subtract this from the mean velocity; if it is in the middle quadrants, add it to the planet's motion. This calculation provides the "Slow-True" velocity <note>original: "Mandasphuta-gati"</note>.

**[Scholarly Commentary]**

239 **She brings [the argument]: "She said to him: I will kill you"** (and it should read: "kill him" [her husband]). He said to her: "Is it not enough that I should be counted with a group of adulterers, let alone that I should be counted with a group of murderers?" And on page 243: "Another interpretation: 'Behold, my master'—he said to her: You seek nothing but sexual relations, etc." The legend that Potiphar's wife wanted to kill her husband and Joseph would not listen to her is hinted at in the Mekhilta there: "'Thou shalt not murder, thou shalt not commit adultery'—[Joseph said] to Potiphar." It is explained more fully in the Mekhilta de-Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai there: "And regarding Joseph it is written: 'How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?' (Gen. 39:9). He said to her: 'Is it not enough that I should be counted with the adulterers, but also with the murderers?'" (This appears to be an added explanation from the compiler of *Midrash HaGadol*). In *Seder Eliyahu Rabbah* regarding "Thou shalt not murder," it says Joseph fulfilled this by not listening to his master's wife and killing Potiphar. See also *Leviticus Rabbah*. Ephrem the Syrian also knew this legend and used it, as did Arabic writers; see Schapiro, *Die jüdischen Elemente in der erzählenden Teil des Korans* (The Jewish Elements in the Narrative Part of the Koran), page 38. In the *Testaments of the Twelve Tribes*, *Testament of Joseph* ch. 7, it is also told that the Egyptian woman said to Joseph: "If you do not want to commit adultery with a married woman, I will kill my husband and marry you."

The Rabbi [Theodor] hinted that Potiphar's wife's claim regarding her husband’s "lying" is also found in *Tanchuma*: "And he said to his master's wife: 'Behold, my master'—he said to her: 'Behold, your husband is before you, for all men are equal.'" See also Josephus, *Antiquities* Book 2, ch. 4, sec. 4. In *Pesachim* 111b, they said that "not all fingers are equal," see there.

**1. He is not [here], etc.** The Holy One, Blessed be He, is not here. In the first edition of *Bereshit Rabbah*, the reading is "He is not great," hinting at verse 9: "He is not greater in this house than I." Joseph said to her: "The Lord is great, etc." (and in MS A the reading is "For the Lord is great," which is Psalms 96:4). Rabbi Abin said: She brought him from room to room and from the inner chamber to the bedroom <note>original: "קיטון" (koitōn)</note> until, etc. He said to her: "If you covered those faces of the idol so it would not see, because you are afraid of it, how much more so am I afraid of the Lord, whose eyes it is impossible to cover!" In MS P and as the *Haggadot of the Yerushalmi* write: "He of whom it is written... you did not cover," which is a more correct version. In the first edition, another interpretation is given: "'Behold, my master'—I am afraid of the one Lord" (hinting that "Behold" [He-Nun] equals "One" [numerical value], see above page 1066 note 5). She said to him: "He is not great—the Holy One is not here who is called 'Great'." From chamber to chamber, room to room in the Jerusalem Talmud. He said to her: "You covered those faces, but He of whom it is written 'the eyes of the Lord, they roam'—whom have you covered? Before Him everything is revealed and there is no hiding from Him." In MS L: "He is not, [he said] Great." Between the lines it is written "by the hand of the Lord" and in another hand "He said to her." *Koitōn* <note>original: "קיטון"</note> in MS L is <note>original: "κοιτών", bedroom, room.</note>. The style "these faces" [Aramaic: *yehaton appaya*] (and in printed editions and MS T: "this face is fitting") is like above on page 23. In most manuscripts and the Yalkut, the verse "the eyes of the Lord... roam [feminine plural]" is cited, while only in MS H is it "roam [masculine plural]" as it appears in the biblical text of Zechariah. (The Mekhilta also uses the feminine plural "roaming"). In MS V the reading is "For the Lord, His eyes roam," and in MS P and MS N "His eyes roam." This verse is actually from 2 Chronicles 16:9: "For the eyes of the Lord roam throughout the whole earth" (see Sanhedrin 38b at the end and Rashi there). However, *Lekach Tov*, *Sekhel Tov*, and *Midrash HaGadol* also cite the verse from Zechariah. The language in *Lekach Tov* is: "'He is not great, etc.' Joseph said to her: 'Behold, my master—I am afraid of the Master of the Universe.' She said to him: 'He does not see you.' He said to her: 'Great...'" Rabbi Abin said: "She brought him into the innermost rooms until she stood him before her bed, and she had [an idol]... above her bed. She took a sheet and covered its face. He said to her: 'The face of this one you can cover, but the face of the Rock of Worlds—it is written: The eyes of the Lord, they roam...'" In *Sekhel Tov* page 243: "Another interpretation: 'Behold, my master'—I am afraid of my Master, that is, the one God. She said to him: 'He is not [here].' He said to her: 'Great...'" The statement of Rabbi Abin is copied there on page 239: "Rabbi Abin said: She brought him into the innermost rooms until she stood him before her bed, and she had an idol engraved above her bed. She took a sheet and covered its face. She said: 'I can cover its face and who will know?' He said to her: 'The face of this one you can cover, but the face of the Rock of Worlds you cannot cover, as it is said: The eyes of the Lord, they roam... Therefore it is written: 'and sin against God'." This implies he explains Rabbi Abin's words as an independent statement. So too in *Midrash HaGadol* p. 584. Rabbi Acha taught that she brought him into her room... and she had her idol engraved above it... He said to her: "You covered these faces, of which it is written 'They have eyes but they do not see' (Psalms 115:5); but the Holy One, of whom it is written 'The eyes of the Lord roam'—how much more so!" In the manuscript of the first edition of *Bereshit Rabbah*, our homily is brought before the verse about "the milk of black goats." The version there is: "Another interpretation: 'Behold, my master'—I am afraid of the Lord. She said to him: 'He is not [here].' He said to her: 'Great...'" The legend that Potiphar's wife stood Joseph before her bed and he replied that he feared the all-seeing God is already found in the book of Philo...

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the divine geography of the Sefirot, specifically focusing on "Eden" and the "Garden" as metaphors for the flow of divine emanation from the highest levels of Thought down to the lower realms.</meta>

# Gate 9

This refers to the language of the **Source**, from which the word and the mystery are drawn. "A river goes out of Eden" <note>Genesis 2:10</note>—meaning, a river emerges from the Source and the Fountain. The term "Eden" <note>Hebrew: *Eden*</note> is related to the expression used regarding Sarah when her "source" <note>a euphemism for her menstrual cycle/fertility</note> had ceased and then returned to her; she said, "After I have withered, shall I have **rejuvenation**?" <note>Hebrew: *Ednah*; Genesis 18:12</note>. This implies that the Source was renewed within her.

We have already explained that "A river goes out of Eden" refers to the Sefirah of **Binah** <note>Understanding</note>. "Going out of Eden" means it emerges from **Chokhmah** <note>Wisdom</note>, which is the mystery of the Source drawn from the **Supreme Crown** <note>Keter</note>. 

"To water the garden" <note>Genesis 2:10</note> means to provide divine flow to the Sefirah of **Malkhut** <note>Kingship</note>. **Binah**, which is the mystery of the River, waters **Malkhut**, which is the Garden, by means of the seven Sefirot: **Gedulah** <note>Greatness/Mercy</note>, **Gevurah** <note>Might</note>, **Tiferet** <note>Beauty</note>, **Netzach** <note>Victory</note>, **Hod** <note>Splendor</note>, and **Yesod** <note>Foundation</note>. This is the mystery of the seven [levels] that exist between the first letter *He* (ה) of the Name <note>the Tetragrammaton, Y-H-V-H</note> and the final *He* (ה). 

From **Malkhut** and below is the **World of Separation** <note>see Sefer ha-Bahir, page 17</note>. "And from there it was parted and became four heads" <note>Genesis 2:10</note> refers to the mystery of the four camps of the **Shekhinah** <note>the Divine Presence</note> that separate from the mystery of the **World of Unity**. This is the mystery of (A) the four letters in Unity, and the "four heads" in Separation.

Now, we must inform you of what is written in the Torah: "The Lord God planted a garden in Eden from the east" <note>Genesis 2:8</note>. (B) How is this possible? For we have said that it [Eden] is the mystery of the world of **Keter** <note>Crown</note>, which is the world of **Thought** that "no eye has ever seen" <note>Isaiah 64:3</note>—so how can you say the Garden is planted *within* Eden? 

(C) Furthermore, our Sages revealed this matter in the chapter "One may not stand" <note>Talmud, Berakhot 30b/34b</note>: (D) Rabbi Joshua ben Levi said, "What is 'Eye has not seen'? This is the **wine preserved in its grapes** from the six days of Creation." Resh Lakish said, "This is Eden, which no eye has ever seen." And if you ask, "Where did Adam live?"—he lived in the Garden. And if you ask, "Is the Garden not Eden?"—the verse teaches: "A river goes out of Eden to water the garden." Thus ends their words.

Contemplate the words of the Master [the author] of blessed memory in this place. He says that Eden is one thing and the Garden is another. If so, how can the literal meaning of the verse be settled? For they did not finish explaining it in the Talmud. 

Here, I will provide a hint: "And the Lord God planted a garden in Eden." He planted the roots of the Garden—which is the mystery of the Sefirah of **Malkhut**—within Eden, which is the mystery of the **Beginning of Thought** <note>Chokhmah</note>. This is because the end of Wisdom <note>Chokhmah</note> and the end of Intelligence <note>Binah</note> are one unified whole. This is the mystery of the "planting." 

How so? The final letter *He* (ה) of the Name has its "plantings" extending into the letter *Vav* (ו), and from there they spread and go until the first letter *He* (ה), and from there they draw nourishment from the letter *Yod* (י) <note>it is known that the *Keter* surrounds the *Yod* and the power of the *Ein Sof* is there</note>, which is the first letter of the Name. This is the mystery of "And the Lord God planted a garden in Eden"—it is a great mystery, hidden and sealed within the four letters of the Name. 

From where is all this drawn? "From the east" <note>Hebrew: *Mi-Kedem*</note>—this is the mystery of the **tip of the Yod** <note>representing Keter, the highest point</note>. A wealthy person <note>or a wise one</note> knows how to direct the path according to the order of the Garden's planting, from the level of the Sefirah of **Malkhut** up to the Sefirah of **Chokhmah**, which is the mystery of the True One. (E) ~~Gate of the matters of my handiwork~~ to be glorified. If you understand what we hinted at in the *Faithful Shepherd* <note>Ra'aya Meheimna</note> <insert>Section 100</insert>, the literal meaning will be settled. What the Sages of blessed memory interpreted regarding it also settles upon "Eden to its ground," as a river goes out from it to water the Garden. The truth is that it is so: Adam lived in the Garden, and not in Eden. (F) And the reason is "Eye has not seen." (G) [This mystery] is hidden within many things in Creation; if you are worthy, you will receive a "drop to the mouth" of deep and sealed traditions regarding them, which we hinted at in the word *Adonai* <note>Lord</note>. The things we have written are merely hints and parables. 

The Sages of blessed memory already hinted at great principles regarding this in the Midrash. You must also consider that there is another difficult verse: "You were in Eden, the garden of God" <note>Ezekiel 28:13</note>, which implies that Eden *is* the Garden. I am now untying the knots of doubt: **Hiram**, king of Tyre, ascended in the Beginning of Thought, which is Eden, and he is the "Grapes." <note>Note: 'Wine preserved in its grapes'</note>. And this is a <margin>hidden</margin> matter.

---

**Commentary (Sha'ar Cheshbon):**

**(A) Four letters in Unity, etc.** This means the four letters of the Name [Y-H-V-H] which are hinted at in the unity of the Sefirot. Correspondingly, in the World of Separation, there are the four winds [directions] of the world, as mentioned at the beginning of the Gate.

**(B) And behold, Eden is for those who say** that it is the mystery of the world of **Keter**, because it is the source of the "workings" there, the world of the Crown.

**(C) Furthermore, the Sages revealed the matter.** Meaning, they revealed that Eden and the Garden are two distinct levels: the Garden is one, and Eden is another.

**(D) Rabbi Joshua ben Levi said: "Preserved in its grapes."** The explanation is that **Binah** is called this because it is "preserved" by itself—Keter and Chokhmah—from any [unbalanced] extension from there. "Preserved" <note>Meshumar</note> is from the language of "guarding" <note>Mishmeret</note>. "Eye has not seen" refers to **Binah**, for it is the guard of the "six days of Creation" <note>the lower six Sefirot</note> that follow it. My understanding is only slight, based on the mention of the "dwelling place" as a model of the [primordial] days. It is also called "Wine" because there is a measure of "Judgment" <note>Din</note> within it. The reason for this is that through it, all the paths that are hidden in the mystery are spread out and revealed to the world, just as wine brings joy. It is the joy of the intellect and the connection...

...these classes should be used as exercises for the hearing and the hand, or as preludes for performing complete melodies and as rests from them.

***

(The Origin of Musical Melodies)

What brought about melodies is an instinctive human nature. Among them is the poetic form, which is instinctive to humans and embedded in them from their very beginning. Among them is the animal instinct through which it vocalizes during certain pleasurable or harmful conditions. Among them is the human's love for rest after fatigue, or not feeling fatigue during work, for humming is something that distracts from fatigue during work so that it is not felt. For this reason, one does not perceive the time during which one performs a task, does not grow weary of it, and persists in it more. For the perception of time is followed by a stronger imagining of fatigue, which makes one feel it, since fatigue only follows movement, and time is a concomitant of movement. Then each of them follows the other, I mean time and movement, for neither is ever separated from the other.

It is also thought that humming might act in the same way on some other animals.

translation:
...the material intellect <note>original: "العقل الهيولاني"</note> and the intellect in act <note>original: "العقل بالفعل"</note>, which is the cause of that thing being imprinted in the material intellect. Through it, the things that were intelligible in potential become intelligible in act, and it also becomes an intellect in act after it was an intellect in potential. The action of this separate intellect upon the material intellect is similar to the action of the sun upon the sight; for this reason, it is called the <term>Active Intellect</term> <gloss>al-’aql al-fa’al</gloss>. Its rank among the separate things that were mentioned, excluding the First Cause, is the tenth rank. The material intellect is called the passive intellect. 

When that which has the status of light for the sight is attained in the rational faculty from the Active Intellect, the sensible objects that are preserved in the imaginative faculty then become intelligible objects in the rational faculty. These are the primary intelligible objects that are shared by all people, such as "the whole is greater than the part" and "quantities equal to one thing are equal to each other." The primary shared intelligible objects are of three types: one type is the principles of scientific geometry; one type is the principles through which one grasps the beautiful and the ugly of what a human being ought to do; and one type is the principles used to know the conditions of the beings that are not within the capacity of a human being to act upon, as well as their principles and ranks, such as the heavens, the First Cause, and the rest...

These are the shining tree of difference, and it is true that "There is no god but..." is the name of the Creator. For the perfection of this celestial subtlety and the illumination of wisdom and the divine face are in the meaning of His saying, the Almighty: **"Actions are by intentions,"** and it is God... and they contemplated, and it is great from a garden, so inhale the thought from the hollow of grace. Reflect, for the sake of the Unity and the secret of duality, for the flooding of human judgments. The appearance of Unity is not valid except after the distinction of the duality, the true [duality] of thought and the interceding secret, not in the secret of the odd. For the intercessor is more creative than he who witnessed the odd in the secret of the intercessor; it has fallen upon the left hand. The happiness is for the nightly stations of the self. Therefore, the day is equal to fifty thousand years in the second complete rank, and by its estimation in the second rank, as the Prophet, peace be upon him, estimated it in his saying: "The Truth rides..." God opened for him the Unity without defining the duality. It was a solar day of a thousand years, and for the dual things, the direction of unity; for its day is like a thousand years. From it is the power of thought over the split. The day of victory is spent in the accidents of deeds... and follow the plan of generosity in the world of joy and beauty by essence. Remove sorrow from yourself, for the Forgiving is Appreciative. The states of the lower limbs in the throat, the system and the decree of material matter appear in the luminous trick in the model of what is in it... It will be in the... and the jewel... as a cause. When it became between the two cycles, it appeared in the tree of generosity for the Truth in the <term>Jabarut</term> <gloss>World of Power</gloss>. It has appeared upon life, and in the interior of the record surrounded by the Truth with heat, in the <term>Jim</term>, in the total with beauty. What He created with unity is in it with the <term>Ja</term>, and its exterior is in the Majesty. In the <term>Jim</term>, Majesty has an impact; it has the secret of subjection in life, a face of the secret by the heart. In the Majesty, it poured between the celestial dimensions and contended for the <term>Malakutiya</term> <gloss>World of Sovereignty</gloss>. The Majesty manifested a light secret for the life of the essence of the intellects, so it spoke a radiant light, an image of existence in the Majesty, the body of Majesty. It is in the Lordship, for the state of the divine Lordship and the illumination is in the manifestation of the Highest Truth. I do not forget the vision of the <term>Jim</term> and its spirit of fulfillment, and <term>tawhid</term> is the origin of wisdom by these considerations. Hence His saying, the Almighty: **"Say, 'Is..."**

...the spirits of the <term>Malakutiya</term> <gloss>Sovereign Realm</gloss> and the lights of the <term>Jabarut</term> <gloss>Realm of Power</gloss> ascend from them. The entire celestial world was lights and the light of lights, which is the <term>Arsh</term> <gloss>Throne</gloss>, and the illuminator of the light is God Almighty, for His saying: **"God is the light of the heavens and the earth."** <margin>Light of the heavens</margin>
The Truth, the first thing He created from His light, were letters of light, their letters by completion in the world of the <term>Malakut</term> <gloss>Dominion</gloss> and <term>Jabarut</term>. That light is after the intellects, and the light of the <term>Jabarut</term> is after the spirits, and the light of the <term>Malakut</term> is after the heart. Thus, the twenty-four were completed, a dictation from eight times eight. Understand that. Therefore, whoever says "There is no god but God, Muhammad is the Messenger of God" for the acceptance of the Throne, it is because the good word ascends by its essence until it has a ratio in the dominion; it goes out into the <term>Jabarut</term>. Its ascent is in the <term>Malakut</term>, so it is not hindered, and nothing of the truths of the worlds issued from it follows it, and it returns to Him. "To Him ascends the good word, and righteous work raises it." Therefore, whoever says it upon seeing the [new] moon, his spirit appears beneath the Throne, so he is nourished by that because of its precedence. Therefore, one of the most important things upon seeing the crescent is safety from all diseases. Whoever says it upon seeing the city is safe from its tribulation. Whoever says it with the intention of marriage in the powers, it is clarified for him therein what he intended. This is all through extracting what we mentioned and correcting what we hypothesized, by perfecting the understanding of the secrets of the letters and the arrangement of the worlds that govern them. As for his saying, **peace be upon him**: "Actions are by intentions, and for every person is what he intended." Since the... are twelve, and everything is stopped by it, the standing ends. That is the hypothesis. He differentiates in the shadows of the letter, and its manifestation is in the day of the <term>Hajj</term> <gloss>Pilgrimage</gloss>. In the <term>Hajj</term>, beauty is hidden in the middle. This reality reveals the secret, so realize its meaning, the Pardon. This is because the <term>Jabaruti</term> ratio for the meaning is with the light of lights. The pole of the circle has settled upon the <term>Muljamiyya</term> Essence, the <term>Mahiyya</term> <gloss>Essential</gloss> attributes, the absolute powers, the appearance of wisdom, and a heart cycle. It became silent and settled, and the intellect loaded with bodies appeared until it descended to the dust, and the night and day were completed after... the souls were supported only in the perfection of the house of <term>Tubaiyya</term> <gloss>Beatitude</gloss> of the Throne, and time is a replacement... the spirits... until the eye of darkness broke for the Chosen One—may his secret be sanctified—in the holiness of that magnificent tree and the noble result when witnessing...

SECTIO VIGESIMA QUINTA. De Papillis et Verrucis in Extre- <margin>SECTIO XXV.</margin> mitate Nasi ortis.

**S**ÆPISSIME oriuntur in extremitate nasi papillæ et verrucæ, quæ indies crescunt et augescunt donec deformis aspectus earum fit. Oportet igitur ut quum primo appareant exscindas et totaliter eradices illas, locoque adhibeas uftionem, vel igne vel medicina urenti quæ cauterii vicem gerat. Quodsi amissa fuerit exscisio donec magnæ fint, confidera quidem, et si verruca lapidescens fuerit, dura, colore fusca, sensusque parvi, ne tractes cum ferro, est enim tumor cancerofus: fæpissime enim vidi mala maxima ex abscissione horum tumorum oriri illis, qui afflicti eis fuerant. Quodsi tumor lenis fuerit tactui, nec colore fuscus, viderisque quod penitus abscindi possit, tum purgato infirmum, et abscinde illum sine metu: et cura locum, deficcantibus et stypticis donec fanetur. <margin>BOOK II.</margin> This is the form of the sneezing funnel <note>original: "infundibulum sternutatorium"</note> with which oils or medicines are dripped into the nose. <margin>SECTION XXIV.</margin>

<note>An engraving of a nasal funnel (infundibulum) with the Arabic word "mas'ut" (nasal dropper) written inside the central bulb.</note>

It should be made of silver or copper, similar to a small lamp, like an oil vessel, open, and its canal constructed in the same manner. And if you wish, you may make the tube closed, like a reed, and the oil chamber of the sneezing funnel is made expanded and open. It has a handle, as you see, by which you hold it when you instill oil, or whatever you wish of juices, or liquid things.

SECTION TWENTY-FIFTH. On Papules and Warts Arising on the Tip of the Nose. <margin>SECTION XXV.</margin>

**V**ery often, papules and warts arise on the tip of the nose, which grow and increase daily until their appearance becomes deformed. It is therefore necessary that when they first appear, you excise and eradicate them entirely, and apply to the area cautery, either with fire or a burning medicine that serves the purpose of a cautery. But if the excision is delayed until they become large, consider the matter; if the wart is calcified, hard, dull in color, and has little sensation, do not treat it with iron <note>the scalpel</note>, for it is a cancerous tumor. I have very often seen great calamities arise from the excision of these tumors for those who were afflicted by them. But if the tumor is soft to the touch, not dull in color, and you see that it can be cut out entirely, then purge the patient, and excise it without fear, and treat the area with drying and styptic agents until it is healed, if God wills it.

<summary>This page describes a nasal funnel for medication and the surgical management of nasal warts, emphasizing the avoidance of surgery for likely cancerous growths.</summary>

R 2-6 Regardless of whether it is state property, legal matters, living beings, or anything else, once it has been placed as collateral <term>gtan-mar</term> <gloss>collateral/pledge</gloss>, the one holding the collateral may maintain and care for it to improve its value. However, apart from the use of the collateral as security for the debt, one may not alter it, raise the tax burden associated with it, or impose any other penalties or collection actions that would harm the asset.

R 2-11 If the property or living being taken as collateral dies, is stolen, or is otherwise lost without the fault of the pledgee, the person who pledged the collateral must provide the full value of the lost item. All debts shall be managed according to the law.

R 3-1 If the property or living being taken as collateral perishes or suffers damage due to misfortune or natural causes, the owner of the collateral is not entitled to its value. Furthermore, regardless of which debt the collateral was intended to secure, the creditor is not entitled to compensation. Both the owner of the collateral and the creditor may not initiate any legal collection actions against each other.

<summary>This page establishes regulations for the handling of collateral, emphasizing that creditors cannot modify or over-tax pledged assets and clarifying liability in the event of the loss or death of collateral.</summary>
<keywords>collateral, debt, property, liability, law</keywords>

Again, in the case where a person has incurred two <term>sanghavasesa</term> violations and, not knowing them to be two, two months have passed, and having concealed them for two months, one was mentioned to the monks and one was not mentioned, the Sangha granted him a two-month <term>manatva</term>. I did not know them to be two, and two months have passed. Having concealed them for two months, one was mentioned to the monks and one was not mentioned. The Sangha granted me a two-month <term>manatva</term>, and as I was undergoing the <term>manatva</term>, I became ashamed.' At that time, the monks asked the Blessed One, and the Blessed One stated: 'Monks, for that person, and for any other person who is similar, grant the <term>manatva</term> based on how the violation was concealed, so that as one comes to know it, it is remembered.'
Again, in the case where a person has incurred a <term>sanghavasesa</term> violation and, not knowing it to be a month, a month has passed, and having concealed it for a month, he mentioned it to the monks, and the Sangha granted him a two-month <term>manatva</term>. While undergoing the <term>manatva</term>, he became ashamed and told the monks: 'Venerable ones, I have incurred a <term>sanghavasesa</term> violation. I did not know it to be a month, and a month has passed. Having concealed it for a month, I mentioned it to the monks. The Sangha granted me a two-month <term>manatva</term>. The treasure revealer who resides as the embodiment of the three mandalas of the wrathful ones; the treasure revealer who is non-dual with the wisdom deities; the treasure revealer who resides as the essence of all the buddhas of the three times.

From the biography of the glorious Padmasambhava: "This biography of mine is the nectar of the speech of all the buddhas; therefore, it should be practiced by those individuals who possess faith." The meaning of what has been spoken in this way should also be practiced by those individuals who possess faith.

<term>Kim Tam</term>, Acting Drafter <term>Yi Su-dae</term>, and Recorders <term>Yi Wi</term> and <term>Hong U-seo</term>. 

<term>Yi Yu</term> said: I have frequently visited the altar site to inspect the work. The completion date is still far off. The labor is extremely massive. From the beginning, the <term>Seogyok Dogam</term> <gloss>Directorate for Stone Work</gloss> was supervised only by the ministers of the Ministry of Rites and Ministry of Works for the sake of simplicity. However, those two ministers each have multiple concurrent roles, such as attending the Royal Lectures or sitting at the <term>Geum-o</term> <gloss>State Tribunal</gloss>. They cannot focus solely on the altar work. Sometimes the office is empty, and only one person is watching the work, which is truly worrying. Although it is difficult to suddenly establish a full <term>Dogam</term> <gloss>Directorate</gloss>, this project is different from others. It would be good to let other officials take over their concurrent duties so they can focus entirely on supervising the altar work. 

<term>Min Jin-hu</term> said: Initially, I was supervising along with <term>Seo Jong-tae</term> and <term>Kim Jin-gyu</term>. Unexpectedly, <term>Jin-gyu</term> was transferred, and I have been handling it alone without a moment’s rest. Now that the Vice Minister of Rites has been appointed, how about ordering him to supervise together? 

<term>Yi Yu</term> said: Regarding <term>Jin-gyu</term>, because the Minister was away, he was made to watch the work. However, because of a single word of mine, he felt aggrieved and did not come out, and then he was transferred. Now there is no need to make the Vice Minister supervise the labor together. It would be appropriate to simply excuse the two ministers from their other duties so they can focus on supervising. 

The King said: Do as suggested. 

<term>Yi Yu</term> said: Directorates are usually staffed by the Ministries of Taxation, Rites, and Works. This altar labor was decided in haste without establishing a formal name.

<sig>Y</sig>

vayan con Dios, que ya esto se ha acabado:
que quedandome sola, y retirada,
mi borrador harè mas descansada.
Por el cabello empieço, estense quedos,
que ay aqui que pintar muchos enredos;
no hallo comparacion que bien les quadre:
que para poco me pariò mi madre!
Rayos del Sol? ya aquello se ha passado,
la Pregmatica nueva lo ha quitado.
Cuerda de arco de amor, en dulce trance?
esso es llamarlo Cerda, en buen Romance.
Que linda ocasion era:
de tomar la ocasion por la molleras;
pero aquessa ocasion yà se ha passado,
y calva està, de averla repelado.
Y assi, en su calva lisa,
su cabellera irà tambien postiza:
y el que llega à cogella,
se queda con el pelo, y no con ella;
y en fin despues de tanto dar en ellos,
que tenemos, mi Musa, de cabello?
el de Absalon viniera aqui nacido,
por tener mi discurso suspendido:
mas no quiero meterme yo en honduras,
ni en hazerme que entiendo de Escritura.
En ser cabello de Lifarda quede,
que es lo que encarecerse mas se puede,
y baxese à la frente mi reparo,
gracias à Dios, que salgo azia lo claro,
que me pude perder en su espesura,
si no saliera por la comissura.
Tendrà, pues, la tal frente,
vna cavalleria largamente,
segun està de limpia, y despejada.

go with God, for this is already finished:
for staying alone, and withdrawn,
my draft will be more rested.
I begin with the hair, keep still,
for there is much entanglement here to paint;

for little indeed did my mother give birth to me!
Rays of the Sun? that has already passed,
the new <term>Pragmática</term> <gloss>royal edict/sumptuary law</gloss> has removed it.
Bowstring of love, in a sweet trance?
that is to call it "Bristle," in good Spanish.
What a lovely occasion it was:
to take the opportunity by the forelock;
but that opportunity has already passed,
and it is bald, from having been plucked.
And so, on its smooth baldness,
its wig will also be artificial:
and whoever arrives to catch it,
is left with the hair, and not with her;
and in the end after so much banging on them,
what do we have, my Muse, of hair?
that of <note>Absalom, the biblical figure known for his long hair</note> could have been born here,
for having my discourse suspended:
but I do not want to get myself into deep waters,
nor make myself out to understand Scripture.
Let it remain as Lifarda's hair,
which is the most that can be praised,
and let my observation descend to the forehead,
thanks to God, I am heading toward the clear,
for I could have lost myself in its thickness,
if I had not come out through the gap.
The said forehead will have,
a large amount of cavalry,
as it is clean and clear.
