Philosophen / Oratoren und Poëten gedenken, welche zwar im Reden sich eines freyen unnd muntern Geistes gebrauchten / und dieselbe ausführlichen vortrügen; jedoch im Schreiben gar kurz und Sinn-reich waren.

Der Sieg-mächtige Cesar schrieb an den Römischen Raht / folgenden Begriffs: *Veni, vidi, vici*, Käiser Octavianus an dessen Batter Cajum Drusum, dieser Masse: Weil du iziger Zeit dich in Ilirico befindest; so gedenke, daß du von Käiserlichem Geschechte bist / daß dich der Senat daselbst so hab hinab geschickt / da du noch jung gewesen / daß du mein Vater bist / und daß du ein Bürger der Stadt Rom bist.

Des löblichen Keysers Tiberii Schreiben / an dessen Brudern Germanicum, contenta waren diese: Die Kirchen seyn versehen / die Götter werden geehret / der Senat ist friedlich / das Vaterland ist in gutem Wolfstand / Rom ist gesund / das Glük ist still / das Jahr ist fruchtbar / und was alhier in Italia vorgehet / wünschen wir euch daselbst in Africa.

Pompejus läßt folgender Masse / wie kurz / also verständlich und sinn-reich / sein Schreiben abgehen an den Raht von Orient: Damasco ist gewonnen / Pempolis bezwungen / Arabia ist confœderiret / und Palatia ist eingenommen.

Cneus Silvius beschreibet kürzlich die Pharsalischen Schlachten also: Pompejus ist umkommen / Ruffus ist geflohen / Cato hat sich selbst erstochen / die dictatur hat ein Ende genommen / und die Freyheit ist verlohren.

20. As I traveled further into the country, I came to a place called Semers, which is to say as much as a city, which lies under a mountain near the city. The mountain is very high to walk upon, especially in winter because of the great snow that lies upon it. Those who do not know the way well, to go up and down, should surely sink into the snow and perish. Therefore, it is better to stay in the place Semers for a month until the snow is off the roads. It was told to me in the city that fourteen or fifteen horses from Italy had arrived there, laden with silk and velvet, to bring the same to the land of Trent <note>original: "Trient"</note>. They were warned of the danger of climbing this mountain because of the treachery of the hidden snow. They asked nothing after this warning; these people traveled on upon this mountain for about half a mile, missed the way, and all together with horses and all their goods tumbled down into the snow and all remained there.

It now moves into the "Samskaras" or life-cycle rituals, specifically focusing on the timing for the bride's entry into the home, conception, the child's first feeding, ear-piercing, the prenatal hair-parting ritual, and the first haircut.</meta>

# Auspicious Timings for Life-Cycle Rituals

The soft constellations <note>original: "mṛdavaḥ"</note>, when combined with the lunar days of *Nandā* <note>The 1st, 6th, and 11th days</note>, *Jayā* <note>The 3rd, 8th, and 13th days</note>, and *Pūrṇā* <note>The 5th, 10th, and 15th days</note>, are highly effective. For all activities, avoid the *Riktā* <note>The "Empty" days: 4th, 9th, and 14th</note> days. The constellations of **Mūla**, **Maghā** <note>original: "pitṛ," the ancestral deities who rule Maghā</note>, **Revatī**, **Mṛgaśīrṣa** <note>original: "śaśi-kara"</note>, **Svātī**, the three **Uttarās**, and **Rohiṇī** are auspicious. When the Moon is in these stars, specifically for the "friend" constellation <note>original: "mitrasya," referring to **Anurādhā**</note>, success is held in the palm of one's hand. **22**

For the <term>Vadhū-praveśa</term> <note>The ritual entry of a new bride into her husband’s home</note>, one should choose the soft or fixed constellations, or **Mercury**, **Puṣya**, and **Mūla**. Also favorable are **Maghā**, **Svātī**, **Aśvinī**, and **Śatabhiṣā** <note>original: "anilam" and "vāmava"</note>. This should be performed on a *Nandā* or *Pūrṇā* lunar day, while avoiding the days of Friday, Sunday, and Tuesday. **23**

Regarding the rite of <term>Ṛtu-dānam</term> <note>The ritual for conception/first union after the menstrual cycle</note>: One should avoid the first four nights and the eleventh night of the cycle. It is best performed when the Moon, Jupiter, and Venus are in strong positions. Even if a son is desired, the ritual must not be performed on the prohibited nights. **24**

The <term>Annaprāśana</term> <note>The first feeding of solid food to an infant</note> should occur in the sixth or eighth month for a boy. The fixed constellations, **Śatabhiṣā** <note>original: "vāri"</note>, **Hasta**, the soft stars, and **Śravaṇa** <note>original: "vaiṣṇave"</note> are recommended. This ceremony is auspicious on the days of Jupiter, Mercury, or the Sun, falling on the *Jayā*, *Nandā*, or *Bhadrā* <note>The 2nd, 7th, and 12th days</note> lunar days. **25**

For <term>Karṇavedha</term> <note>The ritual piercing of a child's ears</note>, the third or fifth month, or the months of Chaitra <note>original: "madhu"</note>, Kārttika, and Pauṣa are suitable. Monday, Wednesday, and the lunar days of *Nandā*, *Bhadrā*, *Jayā*, and *Pūrṇā* are best. The constellations **Aśvinī** <note>original: "dasra"</note>, **Hasta**, **Citra**, **Śravaṇa**, **Dhaniṣṭhā**, **Punavasu**, **Puṣya**, and the three **Uttarās** are favored by the wise. **26**

---

<column-break/>

**Mūla**, **Puṣya**, and **Svātī** are also favorable. On the *Nandā*, *Pūrṇā*, and *Jayā* lunar days, and on the days of Mercury or Sunday, one should perform the <term>Sīmantonayana</term> <note>A prenatal ritual where the husband parts the pregnant wife's hair; intended for the health of the mother and fetus</note>. This should be done when the Moon is strong and preferably when the rising sign is Cancer <note>original: "karka"</note>. **27**

For <term>Muṇḍana</term> <note>The ritual first haircut or tonsure</note>, the months of Pauṣa and Māgha, and the constellations **Puṣya**, **Aśvinī**, **Śravaṇa**, and **Abhijit** <note>original: "śaṅkara"</note> are recommended. The third, fifth, seventh, and tenth lunar days are auspicious, as is the *Jayā* lunar day. This brings prosperity to the child. **28**

For the <term>Āndolana</term> <note>The ritual of placing the child in a swing or cradle for the first time</note>, the constellations **Hasta**, the three **Uttarās**, **Rohiṇī**, **Mṛgaśīrṣa**, **Anurādhā**, **Revatī**, and **Aśvinī** are best. It should be done on Monday or Wednesday, on the *Nandā* or *Bhadrā* lunar days. **29**

For the setting of gems <note>original: "ratna"</note> and the use of medicines like <term>Hingu</term> <note>asafetida, used traditionally for digestive health</note>, the months of Māgha, Chaitra, and Vaiśākha are suitable. The constellations should be swift, soft, or fixed. Avoid the *Riktā* days. This ensures that the medicinal treatments are effective and the gems bring good fortune. **30**

The days of the Sun or Jupiter are favorable for actions involving the constellations **Śravaṇa**, **Dhaniṣṭhā**, **Hasta**, **Puṣya**, and the three **Uttarās**. On Mercury or Friday, the *Nandā*, *Bhadrā*, and *Pūrṇā* lunar days are best for acquiring new clothes and wealth. **31**

For those in their eighth year, the education <note>original: "vidyā"</note> rite is recommended. The months starting from Māgha, avoiding the fifth and eighth, are preferred. Use the constellations **Puṣya**, **Aśvinī**, and **Hasta**...

<meta>This page continues the discourse found in "The Heart of Secrets" (Le Cueur des Secretz), a medieval dialogue concerning natural philosophy. It follows the discussion of the human soul's unique nature compared to other animals and transitions into meteorology (the winds) and astronomy (the sun as the source of all light and the path of the Zodiac).</meta>

### The Heart of Secrets

...other creatures were in service to that creature <note>Refers to humanity, created in God's image as discussed on the previous page.</note>; and thus He gave them a soul such as no other creature possesses, containing all the powers that no other soul has: this soul has even more, for it has a power like that of the angels; it is a **rational soul** <term>rational soul: in medieval thought, the part of the human soul capable of logic and understanding, distinguishing humans from "sensitive" animal souls</term> and yet it is a corporeal beast. It is a great thing that an earthly beast has a rational soul which possesses reason and understanding. This soul is perpetual, so that it shall never die and will always endure. But it is not so with the human body: for it is corruptible, just like the elements from which the body is made. Although *Aristotle* said that generation was perpetual <note>original: "generation estoit perpetuelle." Aristotle argued that while individuals die, the cycle of birth and decay (generation) in the sublunary world is eternal.</note>, this referred to that "generating generation" which is not itself engendered but created—that is to say, commanded. For he says that if God the Creator had destroyed all beasts, each of the parts would return to the element from which it was made. And if He broke apart the elements, they would return to ash. And that ash would, by its nature, produce parts where one is heavier than the other. This thing is done by the will of the Creator and at His command. He meant this regarding creatures of both kinds, because the elements neither grow nor diminish; we will make his meaning more clearly understood to you another time.

Of the souls of men who are endowed with reason and are perpetual, we will speak to you at greater length another time; but we must return to our first subject. Among these things, God made other corporeal things that are called clouds, and yet they are not "animated" <note>Meaning they do not possess a "soul" or life-force like animals or plants.</note>; rather, they are moved through the air by the vapors which are engendered from the sea and the earth by the force of fire and the sun. These vapors are called winds, and they come from the four parts of the world. Each of those which come from the four parts of the world are called **principal winds**, and the ancients gave them principal and proper names, just as we will tell you another time. And they are "principal" because each of these winds has two other winds coming at its side <note>This refers to the classical 12-wind rose: four cardinal winds, each flanked by two collateral winds.</note>. These winds were named (not by the common people). Of the winds, the clouds, their natures, and their powers, we shall treat more at leisure hereafter and in proper order, as it is now necessary for us to return to giving you this answer.

The Creator did one thing when He made that creature which is called the sun: for in making the sun, He made the **day**. And I shall tell you how and for what reason. First, it is necessary to know what "day" is: for day is only the clarity and the glow of the sun. For I tell you—and do not marvel at this—that nothing in the world has brightness, neither fire, nor moon, nor star, except from the sun; and we will speak of this more clearly hereafter. Now listen and accept what I tell you. I tell you that God the Creator made the day bright and shining of itself; and all other things are obscure and dark of themselves. But they receive brightness from the sun, just as I have told you before regarding the **mirror**, which has no brightness except for as much as the day gives it. So it is that the sun and the moon have an established path in the firmament <term>firmament: the sphere of the heavens or the sky</term> which we can see. And that path the astronomers call the **zodiac**; and it is this path which we imagine...

<summary>This page defines the "rational soul" as the unique, eternal trait of humanity and discusses the Aristotelian view of elements and generation. It then explains the origin of winds from vapors and identifies the sun as the sole source of light for all other celestial bodies and the creator of "day."</summary>

These nuns also made for the Inca some pouches that are square, a quarter in size; they carry them under the arm, attached to a very worked braid two fingers wide, placed like a sash from the left shoulder to the right side. These pouches they call <term>chuspa</term>: they served only to carry the herb called <term>cuca</term> <gloss>coca</gloss>, which the Indians eat, which at that time was not as common as it is now, because only the Inca and his relatives ate it, and some <term>curacas</term> <gloss>lords</gloss> to whom the King, out of great favor and mercy, sent some baskets of it per year.

They also made some small tassels of two colors, yellow and red, called <term>paycha</term>, attached to a thin braid one fathom in length, which were not for the Inca, but for those of his royal blood: they wore them on their head; the tassels fell over the right temple.

### Chapter III: The veneration in which they held the things made by the chosen ones, and the law against those who might violate them.

All these things the nuns made with their hands in great quantity for the Sun, their husband. And because the Sun could not wear or carry those ornaments, they sent them to the Inca, as the legitimate and natural son and heir that they said he was of his, so that he might wear them. He received them as sacred things and held them, and his whole Empire held them, in greater veneration than the Greeks and Romans would have if in their paganism their goddesses Juno, Venus, and Pallas had made them. Because these new gentiles, being simpler than the ancients were, adored with the greatest veneration and affection of heart everything that in their false religion they held to be sacred and divine. And because those things were made by the hands of the <term>Coyas</term>, wives of the Sun, and made for the Sun, and the women by their quality were of the same blood as the Sun, for all these respects they held them in supreme veneration. And thus the Inca himself could not give them to anyone else who was not of his royal blood and kinship, because divine things, they said, it was not lawful—it was sacrilege—to employ upon human men. From this, it was forbidden to the King himself to give them to the <term>curacas</term> and captains, however much they had served, if they were not of his blood. We shall speak later of which other clothes of his the Inca gave to the <term>curacas</term> and viceroys, governors and captains, out of the great mercy and favor he bestowed upon them with them.

Besides what has been said, these nuns took care to make at their times the bread called <term>zancu</term> for the sacrifices that they offered to the Sun in the major festivals that they called <term>Raymi</term> and <term>Cittua</term>. It was, it seems, the intention of nature, that those rougher and more unamiable emotions, which drive men from one another, should be less easily and more rarely communicated.

When music imitates the modulations of grief or joy, it either actually inspires us with those passions, or at least puts us in the mood which disposes us to conceive them. But when it imitates the notes of anger, it inspires us with fear. Joy, grief, love, admiration, devotion, are all of them passions which are naturally musical. Their natural tones are all soft, clear, and melodious; and they naturally express themselves in periods which are distinguished by regular pauses, and which upon that account are easily adapted to the regular returns of the correspondent airs of a tune. and leads him; also that it is of the Lord's divine Providence that man should act in freedom according to reason. All this would perish in man if miracles were wrought and he were driven by them to believe. The truth of this may be rationally seen as follows:—It cannot be denied that miracles induce faith, and powerfully persuade men that what is said and taught by the worker of the miracles is true; and that all this at first so occupies man's external thought as, in a manner, to subdue and fascinate it. But man is thus deprived of his two faculties of rationality and liberty, so that he cannot act in freedom according to reason; and the Lord cannot flow in through his internal into his external thought, except so far as to allow him to confirm by his rationality what has been made an article of his faith by means of the miracle. The human mind is so constituted that its internal thought is, as it were, mirrored in its external thought; for, as was said above, a man can inspect his own thought, and this can only be done by means of a more internal thought, and when he sees it as in a mirror, he can also turn it this way and that, and shape it till it appears beautiful to him. The object, if it is a truth, may be compared to a beautiful and living virgin or youth; but if a man cannot turn it in this way and that, and shape it, but only believe it from persuasion induced by a miracle, then, if it is a truth, it may be compared to a virgin or youth carved out of wood or stone, in which there is no life. It may also be compared to an object right in front of the eyes, which alone is seen, and hides from view all that is at either side of it or behind it. Again, it may be compared to a monotonous sound in the ear, which makes one deaf to the harmony arising from other sources. Such blindness and deafness are induced on the human mind by miracles. It is the same with everything confirmed, which has not previously been examined with some degree of intelligence.

Thus, there is the coming-into-being of the organic form and the corruption of the seminal form. These only occur when there is enough "cooking" <note>metabolic processing</note> to decrease the readiness of the matter for the seminal form and strengthen its readiness for the organic form, until the first is removed and the second occurs. 

Here we have two states. The first is prior: the increasing readiness to accept the organic form. The second is subsequent: the attainment of this form. The first state is the action of the **Digestive** power, and the second is the action of the **Nutritive** power. This is the meaning of his saying: "It is digestion," which is the action of the digestive power—the transformations occurring from the completion of the attractive power's action to the beginning of the nutritive power's action. This constitutes a "becoming"—meaning the attainment of the organic form.

Then the Imam <note>al-Razi</note> objected to this, as the author indicated by saying: "It can be said that the force that moves the food toward resembling the organ is the power that delivers it to it." This follows what is in the <term>Eastern Investigations</term> <gloss>al-Mabāḥith al-Mashriqiyya</gloss>: that the digestive power moves the nourishment in "quality" toward the form resembling the form of the organ. Everything that moves a thing toward something else is the "deliverer" to that other thing. Thus, the actor of both actions is a single power. 

As for the minor premise, it is clear because digestion means nothing other than the movement from the "nutritional form" to the "organic form." As for the major premise, it is also clear because whatever moves a thing toward something, the goal of the mover is that destination. By being the goal, the original intention is the realization of that thing. 

Ibn Sina <gloss>Avicenna</gloss> explicitly stated this when arguing that between every two movements there is a rest. He said: "It is impossible for that which reaches a certain limit to reach it without an existing cause that delivers it, and it is impossible for this cause to be different from the one that moved it from its first position." This is his speech. It will follow that since the one that removes the "seminal form" is the Digestive power, the one that delivers it to the "organic form" must also be the Digestive power. Thus, it is the Nutritive power itself and nothing else.

He objected secondly with what the author mentioned: "How can this be? The meaning of the powers here is that they prepare the matter for the 'pouring' of forms upon it." The one who pours the forms is the **Giver of Forms** <term>Wāhib al-Ṣuwar</term> <note>the Active Intellect</note>. The digestive power, through its cooking and ripening, prepares the different readinesses through power—meaning strength and weakness. Among these is that which prepares the matter for the pouring of the organic form. Those powers that prepare these readinesses make other powers in the organs unnecessary. For once the preparation is finished and the readiness is complete, the form is poured and nutrition is achieved. Therefore, there is no difference between the Digestive and the Nutritive powers.

For this reason, Galen <term>Jālīnūs</term> did not mention the Nutritive power in any of his books, except for these four which we called the "servants." Ibn Sina—or rather al-Masihi, according to the *Investigations*—said the nutritive powers are four, and he counted these four among them. The most apparent view is to say: he counted the Digestive power among them when he said in the chapter on "Powers, Actions, and Spirits" in the <term>Book of One Hundred</term> <gloss>Kitāb al-Miʾa</gloss>: "The nutritive powers are four: the Attractive, the Retentive, the Digestive—which is that which changes the food and makes it resemble the nourished organ—and the fourth is the **Expulsive** <term>al-Dāfiʿa</term>." 

Know that nourishment is composed of two substances: one suitable to resemble the nourished body, and the remainder which is unsuitable...

# Preface to the Newly Collected Pronunciation and Meaning of All Scriptures in the Canon

->By the scholar Gu Qizhi<-

The Dharma Master Huilin's secular surname was Pei. He was a man from the kingdom of Shule <note>Kashgar</note>. From an early age, he was steeped in Confucian arts, but upon reaching adulthood <note>the age of twenty</note>, he turned to the Buddhist faith. He studied under the <term>Tripitaka Master</term> <gloss>a title for a monk proficient in the three divisions of the canon</gloss> Amoghavajra <note>the Great Master Bukong</note>. Regarding sutras and treatises, he was especially refined in the study of characters. In the final years of the Jianzhong era <note>around 783 AD</note>, he composed the *Pronunciation and Meaning of the Scriptures* <note>original: "Yiqiejing Yinyi"</note> in one hundred volumes, consisting of approximately six hundred thousand words. It begins with the *Great Perfection of Wisdom Sutra* and ends with the records and biographies of the <term>Hinayana</term> <gloss>Lesser Vehicle</gloss> tradition. At the beginning of our dynasty, the monk Xuan'ying and the scholar Guo of Taiyuan both composed phonetic explanations, but their works were mostly incomplete and brief. However, the Venerable Xuan'chang of Ximing Temple, who was able to continue the great works of his predecessors, labored tirelessly through dark and light. His resolve was as pure as autumn frost, and his mind was as calm as still water. He sought out the lost and overlooked parts of the work, storing them carefully in sandalwood chests decorated with fine embroidery.

aromatic and hot in taste, it is planted by physicians. Pliny and Dioscorides agree. Cassia is of two kinds: cassia fistula and wood-cassia, which is the fruit of something growing near the borders of Babylon. It has diverse species. One is similar to cinnamon, which is reddish and round and has a solid substance, and when it is broken or ground, it does not bend but resists; it is sharp in taste and a little sweet, and this is what provides the virtue. Another is a species that is bitterish, having partially distinct colors, and it has the virtue of the medium; one must choose that which is not easily broken but bends, and which is of a sharp taste mixed with sweetness and aromaticity, being fragile and distinct with whitish interiors and reddish intermixtures. Sometimes it is adulterated when one adds the bark of capers, and they compel it with a bitterish taste. It has a diuretic virtue, that is, a divisive one because of the subtlety of its substance. It also has the virtue of being taken and applied; furthermore, it has the power of strengthening because of its aromaticity. It cures rheumatism and cold causes; it helps those who are epileptic or have the falling sickness; it strengthens the brain; it purges the kidneys and bladder; it ripens and heals apostemes <note>abscesses or swellings</note>; it de-obstructs the kidneys, liver, and spleen; masticated, it removes or cuts off the stench of the mouth; it provokes menstruation and strengthens the womb; it helps with swooning and defects of the heart if a syrup is made from its powder, roses, and the bone of a stag. Dioscorides and Pliny agree.

### Of Cassia Fistula. Chapter XXVIII
Cassia fistula is the fruit of a certain tree that produces long seeds; in time, it elongates and thickens, and through the action of heat, it ripens. The marrow existing inside is black and humid and sweet, and it is mixed with white signs and separated by certain cells in the manner of a honeycomb. One must choose that which is thick and heavy, which shows much humidity in its being; one must also know it should be light and sonorous, which is if it lacks weight and dryness. By virtue, it has the power of softening, mollifying, and cleansing, and it miraculously mitigates the heat of blood and purifies bile and blood. It dissolves apostemes of the throat; it is useful for the viscera and leads out fatty humor; it removes tumors of the viscera and pains of the intestines when drunk. Dioscorides agrees. To which the authors say, as Ovid in the 15th book of the Metamorphoses: "As soon as the cassia and the light ears of nard, etc." And although Pliny and Persius and others say it everywhere.

### Of Calamus. Chapter XXIX

<column-break/>

Calamus is aromatic and is from the Greek; it is named from the similarity to a visual reed <note>a common reed</note>, as Isidore says in Book 17. It is produced in India with many knotted joints, sweet in scent, fragrant with a wondrous sweetness of odor; when it is broken, it is split and divided into many parts. In taste, it is similar to cassia with a gentle, biting acrimony, as Papias says, and it is of a serving virtue. In the gloss on the Eroticum, it is said that aromatic calamus is a species that grows near Mount Lebanon. Dioscorides says it grows everywhere. Pliny says: It is a species that is hot and dry in the second degree. The root of a certain fruit is very similar to calamus and of great odor, and it has a cavity in the manner of a reed in which wood is found, which it extracts; although it is of no value, sometimes one leaves it, and it seems to be of greater weight. The same authors say calamus is of two kinds, namely, that which strengthens the stomach and aids digestion, and that which acts as a remedy for the womb, similar to wormwood. It helps those with cardiac issues and defects of the heart, which the Greeks call syncope, for which it helps much when added to rose water. Pliny says the calamus of odor is Indian and is of the greatest value; it is reddish, full of knots, and dense, and when it is not broken into many parts, it is very dry and is very medicinal, almost like cassia or even cinnamon. Seek the fruit for it also. For it provokes menstruation.

> The Lord of the Month is known by his aspect <note>The astrological gaze or influence</note>; from this, one should declare the good or bad results. Others have stated that the Lord of the Month-Ascendant is the Lord of the Month. || 5 ||

Just as there are five office-bearers <term>Panchadhikari: five planets with specific jurisdictional strengths</term> for the Lord of the Year at the time of the solar return, there are six office-bearers <term>Shadadhikari: six jurisdictional authorities</term> for the Lord of the Month at the time of the lunar return. These are as follows: First, calculate the precise positions of the planets at the moment of the month's commencement. 1. The Lord of the Month-Ascendant. 2. The Lord of the *Muntha* <note>A sensitive mathematical point in Tajika astrology that progresses one sign per year</note> for the month; this is found by multiplying the month number by 2 degrees and 30 minutes and adding it to the yearly *Muntha*. 3. || 3 || 4 || 5 ||

### In the Anushtubh Meter — The wise have likewise spoken of the Lord of the Day and the Lord of the Day-Ascendant. > The wise should declare the results for the Lord of the Month and the Lord of the Day in the same manner as the Lord of the Year. || 6 ||

The intelligent call the Lord of the Day-Ascendant at the time of the day's commencement the Lord of the Day. Its results—whether auspicious or inauspicious—should be declared by the wise based on the consideration of strength and weakness, just as one does for the Lord of the Year. || 6 ||

### In the Shardulavikridita Meter — If the Lord of the Ascendant's Navamsha is aspected by or joined with the Lord of the Ascendant... > ...and if the Moon also views them both with a friendly aspect, then in that month there will be many kinds of happiness and freedom from disease. This result lasts as long as these conditions remain; one should declare the results by calculating the movements of the planets. || 7 ||

If the Lord of the *Navamsha* <term>Navamsha: a one-ninth division of a zodiac sign</term> of the Month-Ascendant has a friendly aspect with the Lord of the Ascendant (or the Lord of the *Navamsha* where the Ascendant Lord is placed), or if they are both in the same position, and if the Moon views them both with a friendly aspect, then during that month, the person will experience various types of physical happiness and health for as long as this monthly influence lasts. In this way, one should declare the results by considering the strength, weakness, and aspects of the planets through mathematical calculation. || 7 ||

<summary>This page details the calculation of the 'Lord of the Month' and 'Lord of the Day' in Tajika astrology, identifying the six planetary authorities and the conditions for health and happiness during a specific month.</summary>

Lors que ce grand *Jague* ou *Guaga* doit faire une expedition militaire, il s'y prépare par un sacrifice avant le lever du Soleil. Deux Magiciens font alors à ses côtés, & une quarantaine de femmes autour de lui, aiant chacune à chaque main la queue d'un cheval sauvage. Elles chantent au son des instrumens qui composent la musique de ce Peuple. Au milieu de l'assemblée on voit un grand feu & sur ce feu un pot de terre, dans lequel est une composition dont ils se peignent les temples, le front, la poitrine, & le ventre, faisant en même tems plusieurs ceremonies, & quelques enchantemens. Cela continue jusqu'au coucher du Soleil. Alors les Magiciens lui remettent le *Casengola*, qui est une forte de hache. En le lui remettant on l'exhorte à déploier sa valeur. Il en fait sur le champ l'épreuve sur un jeune garçon qu'on lui presente & qu'il tue avec cette hache. Quatre esclaves ont le même sort: il en massacre deux à l'instant & fait massacrer les deux autres hors du [a] *Chilombo*. Un autre sacrifice suit celui-là. On égorge dix vaches, autant de chevres & autant de chiens. On repand à l'honneur de l'Idole le sang de tous ces animaux: mais on mange la chair des victimes, & ce festin est accompagné de grandes réjouissances.

Tous les matins avant le lever du Soleil, le grand *Jague* fait sonner le *Gongo*: c'est la generale. Lors que ses troupes font assemblées, il leur fait une harangue pathetique, après quoi on se met en marche; ces harangues militaires font même réiterées plus souvent, afin d'encourager le peuple & l'Armée. On les voit, dit on, declamer du haut d'une maniere d'échafaut avec une force & une éloquence naturelle, qui ne cede en rien à ce que nous lisons des anciens Grecs & de nos guerriers modernes. Ses Capitaines pratiquent les mêmes usages dans tout ce qui est de leur département. Ainsi s'entretient le courage, disons mieux, la ferocité de ces barbares. Quelqu'un manque-t-il de cœur, ou se trouve-t-il assés lâche pour tourner le dos au milieu de la bataille? on le condamne au dernier suplice, c'est à dire à être mangé par ses compagnons.

(b) Tous ceux qu'ils prennent à la guerre font mangés, les uns plutôt, les autres plus tard. La maigreur prolonge leur vie, car il faut les engraisser. In the middle of the assembly is seen a large fire and on this fire an earthen pot, in which is a composition with which they paint their temples, forehead, chest, and belly, performing at the same time several ceremonies and some enchantments. This continues until Sunset. Then the Magicians give him the <term>Casengola</term>, which is a kind of axe. In giving it to him, they exhort him to display his courage. # In Search of the Supernatural
## Volume Six

->Page Seven<-

Below the Temple of **Guan Xiaowen** <note>Likely referring to a local shrine dedicated to a regional deity or an ancestral figure in a specific township.</note> in the local district, a snake died. Two years later, in the autumn, the incident of **Crown Prince Wei** <note>Also known as the "Witchcraft Scandal" of 91 BCE, where Crown Prince Liu Ju was framed for sorcery, leading to a massive bloody conflict and his eventual suicide.</note> occurred; this crisis was initiated by **Jiang Chong**, a man from the state of **Zhao**. In the ninth month of the first year of the **Yuanfeng** era <note>80 BCE.</note> during the reign of **Emperor Zhao of Han**, yellow rats in the state of **Yan** were seen holding their own tails in their mouths and dancing in the center of the palace’s **Duan Gate** <note>The principal or ceremonial gate of a royal palace.</note>. **Jing Fang’s** <note>A famous scholar of the Han Dynasty (77–37 BCE) known for interpreting the *I Ching* (Book of Changes) to explain natural disasters.</note> *Commentary on the Book of Changes* states: "When executions are carried out without investigating the true circumstances <note>original: "誅不原情" (zhū bù yuán qíng).</note>, the anomaly of rats dancing at the gate will appear."

In the first month of the third year of the **Yuanfeng** era <note>77 BCE.</note>, at the south of **Laiwu Mountain** in **Mount Tai**, there arose a tumultuous sound like that of several thousand people. When the common people went to investigate the noise, they found a massive stone that had stood itself up. It was fifteen feet tall and measured forty-eight spans <note>term: <term>圍</term> (wéi); a traditional measurement of circumference, roughly the distance of a person’s outstretched arms.</note> in circumference, and it was rooted deep into the earth. <summary>This page details three supernatural omens from the Han Dynasty: a dead snake prefiguring the Crown Prince Wei scandal, dancing rats signaling the failed rebellion of the King of Yan, and a massive stone at Mount Tai that moved on its own.</summary>

### Shizhou "Half-Day Return" <note>original: "半天回"</note>

The <term>Zhu Tujing</term> <gloss>Zhu’s Illustrated Classic</gloss> states that the "Cow Heaven Return" <note>original: "牛天回"</note> grows in Shizhou. In spring, it sprouts stems one or two feet tall with red spots. By winter, the stems and leaves all wither. Its root tastes bitter and astringent; it is warm in nature and non-toxic. It treats women’s blood-related disorders, as well as the "five strains and seven injuries" <note>Traditional Chinese medical term for various chronic exhaustion syndromes.</note>. Women taking this should avoid sheep blood, chicken, fish, and moist wheat noodles. There are no dietary restrictions for men. <summary>This entry describes the medicinal herb "Half-Day Return" from Shizhou, detailing its preparation with other plants and its use in treating blood-related ailments and chronic fatigue.</summary>

<header>BOOK THREE.</header>

...Albinus and Quintus Martius Philippus were consuls, in the year 568 from the founding of the city, as Livy relates in the ninth book of the fourth decade. But to the magnificence of these works, let the luxury of the baths now be added. It was the custom of the ancients to bathe daily, a practice which, I believe, according to Celsus, contributes to maintaining good health. From this usage, it came about that every citizen, according to his wealth, had private baths. But later, with the growing luxury of the princes, public baths began to be held; indeed, places were assigned that offered the use of bathing or sweating, either by hot waters or by fire, which they called in Greek <term>thermae</term> <gloss>baths</gloss>. Both elsewhere and at Rome, they seemed to be constructed in the manner of provinces, as Ammianus says, in which even the common people might bathe. It was so popular for princes to bathe indiscriminately with the public that Capitolinus reports that Commodus, Gordian, and the younger Galen bathed three, five, or even seven times a day in summer, and twice in winter, and dined in the baths. Women were also admitted, a convenient instrument for pleasure. The baths most celebrated at Rome were the Agrippine, Neronian, Titi Vespasiani, Domitian, Antonine, Alexandrian, Gordian, Severian, Diocletian, Aurelian, Constantinian, and Novatian. These were built at great expense, almost like cities. In them were very ample courtyards, porticos, and in the porticos were <term>exedrae</term> <gloss>recessed alcoves</gloss> containing seats, in which philosophers, rhetoricians, and others who cared for studies sat debating. There was also a <term>palaestra</term> <gloss>wrestling school/gymnasium</gloss> in which athletes exercised. Moreover, there were many places inside skillfully constructed for fostering luxury. To such insane madness do the Roman princes seem to have sought the temptations of all pleasures, with such great expenditure benefiting so few.

Once you understand the nature and character of justifying faith and what Holy Scripture says about it—such as how it unites us with God; how it purifies hearts (Acts 15); how it overcomes the world (1 John 5); how it makes a new man out of the old (1 John 5); how it brings peace to the conscience (Romans 5), makes us righteous, and much more—then you will also be able to answer your fourth question for yourselves. <header>Musa Dezima.</header>
<sig>Y</sig>

vayan con Dios, que ya esto se ha acabado:
que quedandome sola, y retirada,
mi borrador harè mas descansada.
Por el cabello empieço, estense quedos,
que ay aqui que pintar muchos enredos;
no hallo comparacion que bien les quadre:
que para poco me pariò mi madre!
Rayos del Sol? ya aquello se ha passado,
la Pregmatica nueva lo ha quitado.
Cuerda de arco de amor, en dulce trance?
esso es llamarlo Cerda, en buen Romance.
Que linda ocasion era:
de tomar la ocasion por la molleras;
pero aquessa ocasion yà se ha passado,
y calva està, de averla repelado.
Y assi, en su calva lisa,
su cabellera irà tambien postiza:
y el que llega à cogella,
se queda con el pelo, y no con ella;
y en fin despues de tanto dar en ellos,
que tenemos, mi Musa, de cabello?
el de Absalon viniera aqui nacido,
por tener mi discurso suspendido:
mas no quiero meterme yo en honduras,
ni en hazerme que entiendo de Escritura.
En ser cabello de Lifarda quede,
que es lo que encarecerse mas se puede,
y baxese à la frente mi reparo,
gracias à Dios, que salgo azia lo claro,
que me pude perder en su espesura,
si no saliera por la comissura.
Tendrà, pues, la tal frente,
vna cavalleria largamente,
segun està de limpia, y despejada.

<header>Tenth Muse.</header>
<sig>Y</sig>

go with God, for this is already finished:
for staying alone, and withdrawn,
my draft will be more rested.
I begin with the hair, keep still,
for there is much entanglement here to paint;
I find no comparison that fits them well:
for little indeed did my mother give birth to me!
Rays of the Sun? that has already passed,
the new <term>Pragmática</term> <gloss>royal edict/sumptuary law</gloss> has removed it.
Bowstring of love, in a sweet trance?
that is to call it "Bristle," in good Spanish.
What a lovely occasion it was:
to take the opportunity by the forelock;
but that opportunity has already passed,
and it is bald, from having been plucked.
And so, on its smooth baldness,
its wig will also be artificial:
and whoever arrives to catch it,
is left with the hair, and not with her;
and in the end after so much banging on them,
what do we have, my Muse, of hair?
that of <note>Absalom, the biblical figure known for his long hair</note> could have been born here,
for having my discourse suspended:
but I do not want to get myself into deep waters,
nor make myself out to understand Scripture.
Let it remain as Lifarda's hair,
which is the most that can be praised,
and let my observation descend to the forehead,
thanks to God, I am heading toward the clear,
for I could have lost myself in its thickness,
if I had not come out through the gap.
The said forehead will have,
a large amount of cavalry,
as it is clean and clear.

translation:
R 2-6 Regardless of whether it is state property, legal matters, living beings, or anything else, once it has been placed as collateral <term>gtan-mar</term> <gloss>collateral/pledge</gloss>, the one holding the collateral may maintain and care for it to improve its value. However, apart from the use of the collateral as security for the debt, one may not alter it, raise the tax burden associated with it, or impose any other penalties or collection actions that would harm the asset.

R 2-11 If the property or living being taken as collateral dies, is stolen, or is otherwise lost without the fault of the pledgee, the person who pledged the collateral must provide the full value of the lost item. All debts shall be managed according to the law.

R 3-1 If the property or living being taken as collateral perishes or suffers damage due to misfortune or natural causes, the owner of the collateral is not entitled to its value. Furthermore, regardless of which debt the collateral was intended to secure, the creditor is not entitled to compensation. Both the owner of the collateral and the creditor may not initiate any legal collection actions against each other.

<summary>This page establishes regulations for the handling of collateral, emphasizing that creditors cannot modify or over-tax pledged assets and clarifying liability in the event of the loss or death of collateral.</summary>

aan de Vorstenlandsche hoven, waar de traditie inzake den dans beter dan waar ook zich heeft gehandhaafd, worden de *kemanak* (afb. 68 op den voorgrond) uitsluitend geslagen ter begeleiding van de *bedaja-dansen* ¹).

Verder levert ook de omstandigheid, dat het zeven-tal *tjeloering* in den Djocja'schen kraton de pélogschaal draagt, een versterking voor mijne veronderstelling ²). Immers zoowel de *bedaja-dansen*, als die der *serimpi* en evenzoo het gewone *lajoeban*, worden uitgevoerd op *pélog*-muziek (waarbij de hoogst zeldzame uitzonderingen den regel bevestigen) ³). *Pélog* is het echte dans-toongeslacht, gelijk *sléndro* het *wayanggenus*.

...these classes should be used as exercises for the hearing and the hand, or as preludes for performing complete melodies and as rests from them.

***

(The Origin of Musical Melodies)

What brought about melodies is an instinctive human nature. Among them is the poetic form, which is instinctive to humans and embedded in them from their very beginning. Among them is the animal instinct through which it vocalizes during certain pleasurable or harmful conditions. Among them is the human's love for rest after fatigue, or not feeling fatigue during work, for humming is something that distracts from fatigue during work so that it is not felt. For this reason, one does not perceive the time during which one performs a task, does not grow weary of it, and persists in it more. For the perception of time is followed by a stronger imagining of fatigue, which makes one feel it, since fatigue only follows movement, and time is a concomitant of movement. Then each of them follows the other, I mean time and movement, for neither is ever separated from the other.

It is also thought that humming might act in the same way on some other animals.

<meta>This page continues the previous discussion regarding the vanity of worldly pursuits, specifically focusing on the fragility of wealth and the physical consequences of a life of pleasure, framing these misfortunes as spiritual "Crosses."</meta>

->### Chap. VII. On External Crosses.<-

—many goods, *Luke XII. v. 19.* <note>The text completes the biblical quote started on the previous page: "Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years..."</note> A ship has just perished at sea, which was carrying a good and large portion of his fortune; or a major bankruptcy occurs at the bank of Venice, or of Amsterdam: where are his riches? The rich man awakes from his sleep; and he finds nothing in his hands of the treasures he had dreamt of. On another side, it <note>The "Wisdom of the Cross" mentioned on the previous page.</note> places before our eyes a voluptuary <note>A person devoted to luxury and sensual pleasures.</note>, who has consumed his wealth and his health in fine dining and in other pleasures, which modesty forbids naming: Here he is, nailed to a bed, or to an armchair by the gout, which his debauches <note>Historical term for excessive indulgence in physical pleasures, which was commonly believed to cause ailments like gout.</note> have brought upon him: What has become of his pleasures? They have become for him a continual torment and a painful repentance: as many pleasures, so many torments; where one has sinned, there one is punished. But the man sensitive to the ills of the body remains almost always insensitive to the ills of the soul; until finally his time passes, and God's time comes after this life: it is then that one will pay dearly <note>Original: "payera la folle enchere." Literally "to pay the foolish overbid," an idiom meaning to suffer the heavy consequences of one's reckless choices.</note>, and one will read the chapter on Crosses after death.

<summary>This page describes how worldly losses (like shipwrecks or bank failures) and physical ailments (like gout) act as "Crosses" designed to detach the soul from material and sensual idols. It warns that those who ignore their spiritual failings during life will be forced to confront them after death.</summary>
